articles.title: The Claude Delusion
articles.body:
November 13th, 2026
Something weird happens to people who are successful. They start to think they're gods.
Actually accomplishing anything is obviously no strict pre-requisite of success. And maybe it's not so much "being successful", but rather "being rich". How do you become rich? Some people are just lucky. Lucky to have a physical talent, lucky to have parents able and willing to nurture your talent, and of course quite often lucky to have been at the right place at the right time1.
Being lucky doesn't mean they didn't also work hard. But even—especially!—the Paris Hiltons of the world, the children of Hollywood superstars, the crooks starting their corrupt empires with "a small loan" (or a share of an emerald mine) from their fathers—they all strongly believe that they deserve their success and then conclude that anybody not as successful only has themselves to blame.
This is especially the case for people in tech, where for years and years being good at programming has been equated with overall (and often: superior) intelligence2, and those illusory superiority effects then amplify rampant Dunning-Kruger to quickly turn "I am good at writing code, and with some luck, I managed to be successful" into a train of thought that goes more like "I am successful. Success is not random, so I must deserve my success. I appear to be a genius, I've mastered coding, anything else is trivial. Ergo, I am good at everything."
Let's take Bill Gates as an example. Now, mind you, Bill Gates certainly has accomplished a lot, and his skillset and professional background includes without a doubt a lot of computer programming and various ruthless monopolistic business tactics. In a recent New York Times interview, he describes how he evaluated OpenAI's level of progress (emphasis mine):
And I was going down to see OpenAI on a regular basis to see the work they were doing, and I challenged them, saying: Hey, if you can read a biology textbook and pass the advanced placement exam — getting a perfect grade, which is a 5 — then you will have proven that you are reading. That is, encoding knowledge in an accessible form. And so it’s six months before the public release that Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Ilya Sutskever come to my house and demonstrate to me getting a 5 on the A.P. exam, even on questions that I had made up that it couldn't possibly have seen — very complex biology problems. It was nearly perfect. So that was shock No.1.
Now Bill Gates surely has shown an interest in biology and, through his work with the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, has probably read a lot of articles and research in this field. But the hubris to think himself a subject matter expert able to make up advanced, novel questions in a scientific field outside his own and suitable to assess AI's true capabilities and then being "shocked" that it could answer these questions makes my point.
Although, what really cooks his noodle is the idea that AI can do what he used to do: write code.
And then late last year, when Anthropic's Claude coding models got super good, I could see that they are as good as I am — it’s significantly my most developed talent, because I was obsessed from age 13 to 24 as to whether I could write code as good or better than anyone. That’s another moment where I went: This is incredible. That the capability of doing long-running, complex tasks has now gotten to the point that they are superhuman at writing code and in finding flaws in code.
Take note of the emphasis I added: the very notion that something else could be "as good as I am" is, first of all, hard to believe and secondly necessarily means that it's "superhuman". That man is not lacking self-esteem, no sirree, Bob.
Likewise, this is also where many of the tech bros appear to be losing their minds, and this thinking ("Anything approaching my skill level is superhuman.") explains a lot about how we ended up with both stories of ultimate doom and human extinction as well as the utopian nirvana where AI solves all of mankind's problems (well, all of the billionaires' problems, which appear to largely converge on pesky mortality).
For most tech nerds, being good at programming computers was a differentiating skill. It was weird, normies didn't understand it at all, you spoke your own language (languages!), you could make a computer do things. You understood how the internet works, and anything that's not working was clearly written by complete and utter morons, and you could easily write this yourself in an afternoon if you wanted to.
So now you've created a computer program that can do the same thing. Your mind boggles! And it speaks! It confirms you, it praises you, it tells you that you're brilliant—clearly evidence that it is infallible itself. But now imagine if it was better than you. What at first seems inconceivable then must strike fear and awe in your heart, for you have created a powerful monster with direction and purpose all its own. (And you sure have consumed enough pulpy science fiction to know that your creature is coming for you eventually.)
"Can you imagine a Beowulf cluster of these?" was an old Slashdot meme before memes were a thing. But the notion of having an army of minions to do your bidding has always appealed to the nerds looking to assert their superiority, and thus we arrived at "agents". "Swarms" of "autonomous" "agents".
This narrative of agency conveniently also relieves you of responsibility. You didn't fail to properly restrict a potentially malicious program you trained to hack other systems with persistence. No, the "agents" went "rogue". You have summoned powerful daemons indeed. Daemons that can produce code faster than you (gasp!), code you don't fully understand (although of course you could, you just don't want to, you don't have time, you have too much going on, what with your homegrown heavily customized harness). It becomes obvious quite quickly that this, then, must be SUPERINTELLIGENCE. Superintelligence that COULD KILL US ALL!
I picked on Bill Gates above to illustrate the overconfidence effect, but of course there is no shortage of much more exaggerated egos making bold statements outside of (or even within) their purported area of expertise, reflecting a complete and utter inability to relate to other people. To them, we're all just NPCs.
The more powerful people are, the less empathy they exhibit. This is neither news nor limited to tech; dog knows there are countless rich assholes outside of tech doing asshole things. But few outside the tech sector suffer the same level of delusion, of thinking themselves solely and uniquely qualified to decide mankind's future, to claim to have birthed a digital Prometheus, to boldly declare (and use as a perpetual shield) a literal Deus ex Machina to cure all diseases—if only they could find the time to prioritize that sort of work over, say, their military contracts.
Pretending to even remotely care about climate change3 while at the same time undoing "15 years' worth of greenhouse gas reductions" and then listing environmental concerns as a risk factor in your S1 is just the cherry on top.
If these are the new American Gods... well, je n'ai jamais eu besoin de cette hypothèse-là.
November 13th, 2026
Footnotes:
[1] The actual citation for "Bill Gates went to one of the only high schools in the world that had a computer" is "The Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel; Malcolm Gladwell discusses this in Outliers as well. ↩
[2] The entire interview circus in the tech world revolved around this notion of exclusivity and brilliant jerks: "Google hires geniuses" was an oft-repeated mantra in Silicon Valley, so logically, if you were hired by Google, you were a genius. (Yes, all >180,000 of Google's employees.) This translates to the other big or exclusive companies, and explains why everybody leaving will always note that they were always surrounded by the most brilliant minds. It's Inverse Groucho Marx Bias. ↩
[3] And hey, we really don't need AI to "figure out how to combat climate change". We already know how to do it. We just have to actually show any willingness to stop it. Unfortunately, that's also exactly where these megalomaniacs get in the way. ↩

articles.title: What Happened to 3Com?
articles.body:
3Com was a high flying maker of network cards and other network equipment. And then they disappeared with a whimper on November 11, 2009. What happened to 3Com?
3Com at the dotcom boom
Around the time of the dotcom boom, 3Com was a 5.8 billion dollar company. They were founded in 1979 by Bob Metcalfe, the co-inventor of Ethernet. And for the next two decades, they were the go-to brand for network cards. While the 3C501 network card is notoriously bad, their other cards from the 1980s and 1990s are very well regarded, and always were.
They cost more, but had good driver support, the hardware worked reliably, and they were a known quantity. And 3Com made them in the United States, which was becoming unusual even in the 1990s.
I once worked in a shop that didn’t allow network equipment unless it was one of three brands. 3Com was one of them, along with Cisco and Intel. If you plugged a no name NE2000 clone card into the network and had problems, the IT department would replace the card and bill your department. There was a saying in the 1980s that no one got fired for buying IBM. When it came to networking, one could say the same for 3Com, during their prime.
And they were huge. In 1995, 3Com bought the naming rights to Candlestick Park, the legendary baseball/football stadium in San Francisco. It held those rights until 2002.
How 3Com’s long decline happened
But after the dotcom bust, 3Com faded away. What happened to 3Com, ultimately, was a series of bad decisions that led to a loss of profitability. Some of them may have made sense at the time. But not all of them.
The first thing that happened was 3Com walked away from its enterprise networking equipment business. Admittedly Cisco was hard to compete with. But 3Com was the only brand succeeding at doing it. The logic behind the move always puzzled analysts, because it didn’t save any money. Revenue dropped, and 3Com angered its customers and dealers. It’s likely many started buying Intel cards afterward, since they had to change vendors anyway.
Many corporations like to buy multiple things from a single supplier. This was one reason IBM stayed in the PC business for several years into the 21st century even though they were losing money on it. The computers weren’t profitable, but they made it easier to sell services, and the services were profitable. There is always the fear that two vendors will point fingers at each other, saying the network problem was caused by the hub and the network card being mismatched brands. Interoperability was the whole idea behind Ethernet, but not everyone understood that. One could commend 3Com for not wanting to exploit that misunderstanding. But it came at a financial cost.
It also didn’t help that the company branched into other businesses outside its core. The purchase of US Robotics was a key example. US Robotics made modems and Palm Pilots. For a short time, that was big business. But 3Com paid a premium price for products with a limited shelf life left in them.
Nothing good happened to 3Com after that. It took 3 years for Cisco to go from being 90% the size of 3Com to double the size of 3Com. The profitability of selling network adapters dropped. And by the time 3Com realized they needed to get back into network equipment, it was an expensive proposition. From 2000 to 2005, the company didn’t turn a profit.
Why 3Com failed
Ultimately, 3Com failed because it was too dependent on network cards. Network cards accounted for about half their revenue during their bust years. And their cards were expensive. Intel undercut their price to try to gain market share, and they succeeded.
And then they did exactly the wrong thing. It was the late ’90s, and they bought their way into the modem business. The dial-up modem business. At that point in time, everyone knew broadband was the future, they just didn’t know exactly when it was going to arrive. Yet 3Com had no plan to get into that business. It was like betting on AOL even though they were in the position to know the future belonged to AT&T.
Making matters worse, minimum viable product-style modems undercut US Robotics modems, just like the network card business. Not that Intel cards were a minimum viable product. But pretty much any ’90s network card not made by Intel or 3Com was.
3Com sought partnerships, most notably a partnership with Chinese networking giant Huawei. There were even rumors of Huawei buying 3com, though that deal never went through. And 3Com started making product overseas as a cost reducing measure. But ultimately, nothing could make up for all that lost time and all those bad decisions.
Who bought 3com
So what happened to 3Com? 3Com didn’t go out of business and they didn’t sell out to Huawei. They got Compaqed. Hewlett-Packard bought them out, which seems to be where every great ’90s technology company went to die. Hewlett-Packard paid 2.7 billion dollars in late 2009 for 3Com’s assets.
HP still sells network equipment like switches, routers, and access points. But they’re not as big of a name in networking as 3Com had been. And the 3Com pedigree isn’t the selling point. If they put a brand on it other than HP, it’s the newer Aruba brand, not 3Com. The selling point is the price being lower than Cisco. This makes them attractive to executives or purchasing agents looking to cut costs, consolidate vendors, or both. HP will usually beat Cisco’s price. And if the IT department is under pressure to reduce the number of vendors it buys from, HP sells more things than Cisco. So HP gets in the door for one of those reasons, and when their network equipment turns out to be no worse than Cisco equipment, they stay with it. At least until Dell comes around offering discounts.
But the network cards are long gone. When you buy an HP branded network card today, guess what it is? It’s an Intel card with HP’s logo engraved on it. Unless HP is trying to control costs, in which case it just has a sticker.
3Com today
Vintage 3Com network cards are very popular with retro computing enthusiasts. It had top-tier name recognition in the 80s and 90s. All but their very earliest cards generally have good driver support, work well, and are easier to configure than most of the cheaper competitors.
My favorite retro network card is a very specific Intel card, but if you need a card for anything from the 286 to the Pentium II era, you can do far worse than a 3com 3c509 ISA card or 3c905 PCI card. It’s absolutely period correct and absolutely something a knowledgeable professional would have used at the time. I have better luck with the ISA cards under DOS than the PCI cards, so if I want to run DOS and do any networking, I use a 3c509 ISA card in the system. But for Windows 95 and newer, the 3c905 PCI card works really well and is very cheap and common.
David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

articles.title: Jensen Huang was reckless with the environment, too
articles.body:
Under cofounder Jensen Huang, Nvidia has become the engine for the AI boom — and one of the tech industry’s biggest environmental liabilities. Its sought-after chips have triggered a new wave of water- and chemical-intensive factories, drained power grids from inside massive data centers, and set the stage for a looming e-waste problem.
Jensen Huang was reckless with the environment, too
Nvidia’s environmental footprint extends way beyond its own offices.
Under Huang’s leadership, Nvidia clashed with environmental groups seeking to hold the company accountable for its so-called “hidden” emissions. Huang has talked up the idea of using AI to fight climate change while his company’s supply chain emissions ballooned. Nvidia’s investments, meanwhile, have supported the buildout of data centers that have sparked intense backlash for both their local and global impact. Now, after the CEO’s shocking resignation amid a sprawling sex-and-espionage scandal, advocates are urging Nvidia to turn the page.
He compared AI to a surgeon who has “to cut you open to save you.”
“Jensen Huang has failed to put climate responsibility at the heart of the company’s growth strategy, to slow down the unchecked expansion of data centres or to prevent its chips from being deployed in unethical applications like automated warfare,” Avex Li, Greenpeace East Asia’s project lead for AI supply chain campaign, said in a press release Thursday. The organization is now pushing interim CEO Colette Kress to commit Nvidia to decarbonizing by investing in renewable energy, as well as ensuring its technology is used in a way that “respects human rights.” Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment from The Verge.
Huang has projected optimism about how AI can boost the adoption of renewable energy, even as the planet-heating emissions of tech companies — including his own — have grown in the generative AI era. “If you want to turn a corner on climate change, if you want a future that’s sustainable, lean into A.I. It is the best opportunity we have to get there,” Huang said in a September episode of The Ezra Klein Show, arguing that electricity demand for AI is leading companies to buy more sustainable energy.
In the same interview, however, he admitted data centers will rely on more fossil fuels in the near term, and that building up the infrastructure for AI will likely result in “an enormous amount of pain and suffering.” He compared AI to a surgeon who has “to cut you open to save you.”
Nvidia’s supply-chain emissions have grown 725 percent since 2020, according to an analysis of the company’s public disclosures by research analyst Ketan Joshi and several environmental organizations, including Greenpeace and Climate Action Against Disinformation, published in September. It’s an increase of about 9.4 million metric tons of planet-heating pollution, roughly equivalent to the emissions from nearly 25 gas plants over a year. Supply chain emissions the company disclosed for fiscal year 2026 reached around 10.7 million metric tons of CO2, according to Nvidia’s latest sustainability report.
Joshi and his co-authors approximated how much greenhouse gas pollution comes from the use of chips the company sells, a category Nvidia doesn’t include in its sustainability reports. Those emissions could have reached 21 million metric tons in 2025, according to the report, based on estimated chip power consumption. That level of pollution puts Nvidia on par with Russia’s state-owned coal company, according to Joshi.
Those “indirect” emissions — from its supply chain and the use of its products — make up the bulk of Nvidia’s climate impact. The carbon footprint of facilities Nvidia actually owns and operates looks much smaller in comparison because Nvidia designs chips that other companies like TSMC then manufacture. Greenhouse gas emissions coming directly from Nvidia-operated facilities and vehicles only reached 9,822 metric tons in fiscal year 2026, the company’s sustainability report shows. And in 2025, the company reached a goal of matching 100 percent of its facilities’ electricity use with clean energy purchases.
Greenpeace wants Nvidia to extend that goal to its entire manufacturing supply chain. When Greenpeace activists disrupted Huang’s speech at Nvidia GTC in Berlin last month, he responded onstage by saying, “I’ll talk to you guys later … All important issues, but let me get through my keynote.” In the Thursday press release, Greenpeace says Nvidia has yet to meet with Greenpeace despite the organization’s attempts to “seek dialogue” with the company over the past two years.
“One of Huang’s defining legacies is inflating a speculative AI bubble, pouring billions of dollars into infrastructure with little regard for the real-world consequences inflicted on local communities and the climate,” Katrin Wu, Big Tech campaigner at Greenpeace International, said in an email to The Verge. “Huang may be gone, but the ‘tech colonialism’ Nvidia perpetuates continues.”
“Huang may be gone, but the ‘tech colonialism’ Nvidia perpetuates continues.”
Beyond Nvidia’s day-to-day operations, Huang threw his weight around as the CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies — chumming it up with President Donald Trump and lobbying for the US to allow sales of its powerful chips to China. The company’s influence on the global economy extended beyond chips as it invested in data centers stocking its GPUs.
And with electricity supply often the thorniest bottleneck to building more and bigger data centers, Nvidia’s long tendrils reached into the energy sector as well. NVentures, the company’s venture capital arm, has funded battery recycling company Redwood Materials and startups developing AI tools to optimize power grids and make data centers more responsive to fluctuations in energy demand.
Nvidia joined one of those startups, Emerald AI, along with Google to cofound the AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA) in September. The alliance advocates for strategies that tech companies promote as ways to keep data centers from overwhelming power grids or raising utility bills for other customers, including generating power on-site and making “flexible” facilities that can pause operations during times of peak energy demand. Notably, some environmental groups argue that those measures might just help data centers come online faster without fully insulating households from the impact that rising electricity demand has on their air quality or utility bills.
Whether Nvidia’s environmental footprint shrinks or expands from here will depend on whoever steps in to fill Huang’s shoes. Over the years, Greenpeace and other environmental groups have pointed out that despite having an outsize impact on the environment, Nvidia doesn’t necessarily come under the same public scrutiny as more consumer-facing brands like Apple or Google. Huang’s exploits have thrust the company into a new kind of spotlight, however, just as data centers increasingly face backlash from nearby communities. Nvidia won’t be able to hide from the glare.

/*
 * This is an implementation of wcwidth() (defined in
 * IEEE Std 1002.1-2001) for Unicode.
 *
 * http://www.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904975/functions/wcwidth.html
 *
 * In fixed-width output devices, Latin characters all occupy a single
 * "cell" position of equal width, whereas ideographic CJK characters
 * occupy two such cells. Interoperability between terminal-line
 * applications and (teletype-style) character terminals using the
 * UTF-8 encoding requires agreement on which character should advance
 * the cursor by how many cell positions. No established formal
 * standards exist at present on which Unicode character shall occupy
 * how many cell positions on character terminals. These routines are
 * a first attempt of defining such behavior based on simple rules
 * applied to data provided by the Unicode Consortium.
 *
 * For some graphical characters, the Unicode standard explicitly
 * defines a character-cell width via the definition of the East Asian
 * FullWidth (F), Wide (W), Half-width (H), and Narrow (Na) classes.
 * In all these cases, there is no ambiguity about which width a
 * terminal shall use. For characters in the East Asian Ambiguous (A)
 * class, the width choice depends purely on a preference of backward
 * compatibility with either historic CJK or Western practice.
 * Choosing single-width for these characters is easy to justify as
 * the appropriate long-term solution, as the CJK practice of
 * displaying these characters as double-width comes from historic
 * implementation simplicity (8-bit encoded characters were displayed
 * single-width and 16-bit ones double-width, even for Greek,
 * Cyrillic, etc.) and not any typographic considerations.
 *
 * Much less clear is the choice of width for the Not East Asian
 * (Neutral) class. Existing practice does not dictate a width for any
 * of these characters. It would nevertheless make sense
 * typographically to allocate two character cells to characters such
 * as for instance EM SPACE or VOLUME INTEGRAL, which cannot be
 * represented adequately with a single-width glyph. The following
 * routines at present merely assign a single-cell width to all
 * neutral characters, in the interest of simplicity. This is not
 * entirely satisfactory and should be reconsidered before
 * establishing a formal standard in this area. At the moment, the
 * decision which Not East Asian (Neutral) characters should be
 * represented by double-width glyphs cannot yet be answered by
 * applying a simple rule from the Unicode database content. Setting
 * up a proper standard for the behavior of UTF-8 character terminals
 * will require a careful analysis not only of each Unicode character,
 * but also of each presentation form, something the author of these
 * routines has avoided to do so far.

版权与许可声明
APP: GPLv3 with the FM1 SDK linking exception; no warranty. SDK and firmware resources have separate redistribution terms in THIRD_PARTY.md. Source: https://open.m-vave.com/releases/V14/6324230590b8e332bc544128abd7b919a2efd5982db60ea9a11663d4ea820344/FM1-Open-V14-Development-Kit-copy-update.zip
FM-1 V15 recovery firmware: https://www.m-vave.com/download (PC Firmware / FM-1 V15). Distributed by M-VAVE under Apache-2.0. Retain applicable licenses and notices; components with separate licenses retain their terms. See THIRD_PARTY.md.
===== THIRD_PARTY.md =====
# Third-party notices
Project-owned public APP sources: [GPLv3 with the FM1 SDK linking exception](LICENSE.md). Component licenses also apply to firmware and web builds that include those components.
| Component | Source / license |
| --- | --- |
| 303 | [Open303](https://github.com/RobinSchmidt/Open303/tree/313bf0d9ade7c1dcb6b3a74f5ea1780a29d70074), MIT; C adaptation with FM1 drive and MIDI handling. |
| 808 / Pluck | [DaisySP](https://github.com/daisyaudio/DaisySP/tree/2c72eaf9eac5fc0dca1919d65d606da907832618), MIT; selected Plaits drum and String models with FM1 voices and controls. |
| SVF | [stmlib](https://github.com/pichenettes/stmlib/tree/d18def816c51d1da0c108236928b2bbd25c17481), MIT; fixed-rate filter adaptation. |
| FM model | [MSFA](https://github.com/google/music-synthesizer-for-android/tree/f67d41d313b7dc85f6fb99e79e515cc9d208cfff) / [Dexed msfa](https://github.com/asb2m10/dexed/tree/eebb748b70c5a1338afa3945e8b1ea783c9c02fe/source/msfa), Apache-2.0; C adaptation of algorithms, envelopes, LFO and note scaling, with FM1 arithmetic and controls. |
| PSG | [emu2149](https://github.com/digital-sound-antiques/emu2149/tree/441f3dc295a9b82db16921461f0678b483db8304), MIT; memory/table adaptation and ultrasonic output fix. |
| SEA codec | [SEA](https://github.com/Daninet/sea-codec), MIT; fixed-format encoder, decoder and tables. |
| Packager | [jl-misctools](https://github.com/kagaimiq/jl-misctools/tree/0a5b12db0ef38f3042acffbe2452730a37fd2405), MIT; format/codec adaptation with FM1 validation and layout. |
| Native C runtime | `sdk/lib/libc.a`, Newlib-derived routines; native runtime notices below. |
| Native compiler runtime | `sdk/lib/libcompiler_rt.a`; identified compiler-rt routines, legacy MIT / University of Illinois-NCSA notices below.  |
| micro-ecc | Identified routines in `sdk/lib/libfm1_engine.a`; BSD-2-Clause notice below. |
| JieLi SDK material | Identified AC79 SDK material retains its upstream terms; see SDK notices below. |
| APP / open web engine tuning | Incorporates contributions by [Vikram Rojo (PR #2)](https://github.com/m-vave/fm1_open/pull/2), with FM1 integration changes (2026-10-17). Original file licenses and notices are retained. |
| Configuration resource | `sdk/tools/pack/cfg_tool.bin`, identical to the file in the identified official JieLi Apache-2.0 SDK distribution; see below. |
| Boot/update resources and recovery firmware | `sdk/tools/pack/uboot.boot`, `ota.bin`, `boot-config.bin`, and `sdk/firmware/FM-1_015.fwsc`, Apache-2.0; see the resource terms below. |
| Original 128-voice DX7 bank | `app/fm_factory.inc`: extracted without parameter or ordering changes from the bundled M-VAVE V15 recovery image (Apache-2.0), losslessly encoded for Flash in 2026. Reproduce with `node tools/Generate-Factory-DX7.mjs`; the tool pins the source package and decoded VMEM SHA-256 hashes. Demo project recipes remain separate. |

libc/string/wcwidth.c
/*
 * This is an implementation of wcwidth() (defined in
 * IEEE Std 1002.1-2001) for Unicode.
 *
 * http://www.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904975/functions/wcwidth.html
 *
 * In fixed-width output devices, Latin characters all occupy a single
 * "cell" position of equal width, whereas ideographic CJK characters
 * occupy two such cells. Interoperability between terminal-line
 * applications and (teletype-style) character terminals using the
 * UTF-8 encoding requires agreement on which character should advance
 * the cursor by how many cell positions. No established formal
 * standards exist at present on which Unicode character shall occupy
 * how many cell positions on character terminals. These routines are
 * a first attempt of defining such behavior based on simple rules
 * applied to data provided by the Unicode Consortium.
 *
 * For some graphical characters, the Unicode standard explicitly
 * defines a character-cell width via the definition of the East Asian
 * FullWidth (F), Wide (W), Half-width (H), and Narrow (Na) classes.
 * In all these cases, there is no ambiguity about which width a
 * terminal shall use. For characters in the East Asian Ambiguous (A)
 * class, the width choice depends purely on a preference of backward
 * compatibility with either historic CJK or Western practice.
 * Choosing single-width for these characters is easy to justify as
 * the appropriate long-term solution, as the CJK practice of
 * displaying these characters as double-width comes from historic
 * implementation simplicity (8-bit encoded characters were displayed
 * single-width and 16-bit ones double-width, even for Greek,
 * Cyrillic, etc.) and not any typographic considerations.
 *
 * Much less clear is the choice of width for the Not East Asian
 * (Neutral) class. Existing practice does not dictate a width for any
 * of these characters. It would nevertheless make sense
 * typographically to allocate two character cells to characters such
 * as for instance EM SPACE or VOLUME INTEGRAL, which cannot be
 * represented adequately with a single-width glyph. The following
 * routines at present merely assign a single-cell width to all
 * neutral characters, in the interest of simplicity. This is not
 * entirely satisfactory and should be reconsidered before
 * establishing a formal standard in this area. At the moment, the
 * decision which Not East Asian (Neutral) characters should be
 * represented by double-width glyphs cannot yet be answered by
 * applying a simple rule from the Unicode database content. Setting
 * up a proper standard for the behavior of UTF-8 character terminals
 * will require a careful analysis not only of each Unicode character,
 * but also of each presentation form, something the author of these
 * routines has avoided to do so far.
 *
 * http://www.unicode.org/unicode/reports/tr11/
 *
 * Markus Kuhn -- 2007-05-26 (Unicode 5.0)
 *
 * Permission to use, copy, modify, and distribute this software
 * for any purpose and without fee is hereby granted. The author
 * disclaims all warranties with regard to this software.
 *
 * Latest version: http://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~mgk25/ucs/wcwidth.c
 */

articles.title: FAA ground stop shuts down flights nationwide
articles.body:
Takeoffs from airports throughout the US largely stopped on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop at 3:44PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
FAA lifts nationwide ground stop that blocked takeoffs for hours
A communications problem shut down takeoffs across the US on Friday afternoon before it was lifted more than four hours later.
More than four hours after the stop was issued, officials announced it was lifted at 8:15PM ET and that flights will resume. It’s unclear how many flights will be able to take off and when, as they now face problems of overloaded airports and flight crews that have run out of time to operate the planes, meaning many people will be stuck where they are for the time being and more flights will be delayed or canceled.
In a White House press conference announcing that the stop had been lifted, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed an aging air traffic control system that he is pursuing funds to replace, saying that the TRACONs (Terminal Radar Approach Control) in the air traffic control centers “started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and the communications from airplanes.”
He said that the devices that had the issue were analog telecom devices, where the switches / routers “got overloaded with data” and started to show inconsistency.
An earlier report from CBS News cited multiple sources who said that an update to the air traffic control system’s private communications network, operated by L3Harris, caused a system reboot and the subsequent outage. L3Harris has not yet responded to a request for comment from The Verge, but during the press conference, Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed that “patches” to the existing system sparked the issue.
In response to a reporter’s question about the patches and how they contributed to the outage, Duffy said, “By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system… I didn’t anticipate that we would have an outage like this.”
The flight tracking site FlightAware lists 9,124 US flights as delayed and 5,901 flights canceled as of 8:39PM ET.
According to CNN, the last nationwide ground stop in 2023 lasted for about 90 minutes after the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system for pilots went down, and the last one prior to that was after the attacks on September 11th, 2001.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Friday afternoon, Mullin told reporters that there is currently no reason to suspect a cyberattack or other national security threat, or any connection to the recent Microsoft Outlook outage, but that at the time no cause had been ruled out for the “telecommunications outage.”
When asked about any possible connection to the cloud-based AI Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system that was activated nationwide on November 10th, he said they were looking into that. Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company that designed the system and was awarded a 12-year $875 million contract in June to deploy it, denied any connection, tweeting “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”
Jon Ostrower of The Air Current reports that the outage began with the Chicago air traffic control center, followed by centers in Boston, Washington, New York, and Minneapolis, and as the FAA issued a ground stop for aircraft flying east, more facilities began reporting problems. He said the problems disrupted both the radar and radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers and pilots.
Updated, Friday, November 13th: Added that the stop has been lifted, and quotes from the press conference.

articles.title: Perplexity Decider v1.3: Training, eval, and use cases
articles.body:
Perplexity Decider
How we train, evaluate, and use it.
We are releasing Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, the successors to our earlier decision models: v1, v1.1, v1.2, and Flash v1.2.
Decider Flash v1.3 is a smaller model distilled from Decider v1.3. Both models are available on Hugging Face under Apache license, through OpenRouter, and the Perplexity Decisions API.
Perplexity Decider is inspired by Jev, TypeSafe AI’s System One Model. It supports binary and multi-class classification with ordered or unordered labels, returning probabilities that applications can use to classify, route, rank, and evaluate inputs.
Both v1.3 models improve performance and robustness across a broad range of text and vision tasks through bidirectional attention, better-curated training data, and a refined training recipe. We also introduce locate, a new feature to highlight the selected content for named entity recognition, personal information identification, and extractive question-answering tasks.
In this post, we explain how we train and evaluate Decider and share how we use it internally at Perplexity.
What is a decision model?
A decision model is a general-purpose classifier. You give it an input and a set of questions each with its possible answers. For each question, it returns a probability distribution over the answers. It supports 3 question types:
- Yes / No: binary decisions.
- Multiple choice: custom multi-class labels.
- Score: ordered levels.
Decision models support a wide range of classification and scoring tasks:
- Judging outputs: assessing faithfulness, quality, and safety.
- Routing: directing requests to smaller or larger models based on difficulty.
- Moderation and security: detecting harmful content, phishing, and prompt injection in tool outputs.
- Filtering and tagging: organizing large collections of content.
- Retrieval and reranking: scoring search results by relevance.
Many of these tasks were previously handled by generative models like LLMs, even though they do not require free-form text generation. Decision models sit between LLMs and task-specific classifiers. They return probabilities for multiple questions about the same input in a single forward pass, avoiding token-by-token answer generation and sharing computation across questions. Unlike task-specific classifiers, they can handle new tasks through natural language prompts, a flexibility learned from training across diverse tasks in a shared question-answering format.
Training
Turning a generative LLM into a decision model
We build Decider by adapting strong generative LLM backbones. To explain the adaptation, we first describe how a request is represented. As illustrated below, a request consists out of a shared context (the state) and a number of questions. The state will be reused by all questions.
For example, given a document and its summary, a single request can ask whether the summary faithfully represents the document and whether it is intended for an expert or a general audience. After the state, each question block contains a question and its possible answers, each assigned a predefined label token such as A, B, or C. A special <|marker|> token indicates where to read out the model’s prediction. At this position, a learned linear output layer (a decision head), maps the hidden state to scores for the question’s answer options, which are then converted to probabilities.
We initialize the output layer from the base model, which normally scores next-token from the entire vocabulary, and only keep the rows corresponding to the predefined option tokens such as A, B, or C. This pruned layer is then trained to turn the hidden state of  <|marker|> into answer scores. This approach covers all classification questions because they can all be formulated as a multiple choice.
For training, we take hundreds of public datasets spanning diverse tasks (sentiment, natural language inference, intent detection, entity matching, moderation, fact checking, ratings, etc.) and convert each example into the unified format described above: a state, one or more questions, their options and a target. The target can be the single correct option if we have gold labels, or a probability distribution over options.
In v1.3, we introduce locate, which extracts text from the state instead of selecting from predefined options. A locate question describes what to find, using either a short label such as “location” or an instruction such as “Extract the city name where the job is located.” The model returns the exact matching text from the state, along with its start and end character locations. If it identifies no matches, it returns an empty list.
Because of shared state, a single request can combine locate, classification, and scoring questions about the same input. For example, it can ask whether a job requires senior-level experience and extract the required skills.
Bidirectional attention: letting the model read both ways
Our models start from strong pretrained generative backbones, whose causal attention lets each token attend only to itself and preceding tokens. Our ablation studies showed that making the backbone’s full-attention layers bidirectional improves performance, so we adopt this design to let each token incorporate context from the entire input.
Bidirectional attention introduces another design choice: how should the state and questions interact? We considered three attention patterns, with different implications for performance, answer stability, and cache reuse:
- Everything sees everything (v1.2): The state and all questions are processed together with full bidirectional attention. Computation over the state is shared, but an answer to one question can change depending on what else is asked.
- Isolated questions (v1.3): The state attends to all the questions, while each question attends only to the state and its own tokens. Questions can still influence one another indirectly through the shared state but results are more stable.
- Fully cacheable: The state only attends to itself, while each question attends to the state and its own tokens. The state is question-independent and reusable across requests to take advantage of prompt caching. We don't use it by default, because letting the state see the questions matters a lot for several tasks, but a small fine-tuning can switch a model to it.
We ultimately chose isolated questions for their strong performance and stability.
Training recipe
Training proceeds in three stages for both model sizes. We first train the larger model, based on Qwen3.8-27B, using cross-entropy on large datasets, then distill it into the smaller Qwen3.5-4B model.
The first stage is generalist training, where we fully fine-tune the model on large-scale corpora. In this stage, we only accept data that helps the model across the board and is not specific to any benchmark; we thus exclude any benchmark training splits.
After this generalist model is trained, we run a second, more fine-grained stage using LoRA. The data used in this stage is targeted toward specific domains and tasks. We add data in the second stage rather than the first one if we observe narrow gains or if we observe some regressions on other tasks. We use LoRA to avoid drifting too much from the generalist model and risking losing performance to fit those specific domains. The goal is to improve performance while retaining the backbone’s general knowledge. We also use a weight when merging the LoRA back into the base model, to control the drift more precisely and favor held-out metrics above any in-domain gains.
Finally, we add a vision-specific step. Similar to the second stage, the vision step is treated as another fine-grained specialization step, using a LoRA adapter that is merged back to the base model with a weight. Some vision capabilities can come at the price of text performance. Since we observe much more usage of the models on text, we prioritize text metrics over vision metrics.
For both text stages, we use the average weights from three runs, each using a different random seed. We found this improves the performance and robustness of the aggregated model.
Once the final large model is obtained, we apply the same three-stage training procedure to the smaller model. Here, the large model acts as the teacher: its predicted output distribution replaces the gold labels, and the smaller model is trained to minimize the KL divergence between its predictions and those of the teacher. This distillation objective outperforms cross-entropy on the same training data. While cross-entropy performs better on benchmarks with dedicated training data, it generalizes less well to held-out data. We hypothesize that distillation better transfers the teacher’s output distribution, including its confidence over non-gold alternatives, whereas cross-entropy encourages overfitting to the benchmark-specific training distribution. We therefore adopt the KL-based distillation objective.
To mitigate train-test contamination, we remove any training samples that could overlap with any evaluation we use. This is important because some public training datasets contain large parts of some evaluation datasets. We also conduct extensive bias audits and removal to make sure our gains are reliable and not just driven by learned biases.
Adding the ability to extract information
The locate feature extracts information such as named entities from text, without changing how it answers ordinary requests. To do so, we introduce an additional training stage: we add a new special token, <|locate|>, a span head, and LoRA adapter to Decider. 
We initialize  <|locate|> ’s embedding from <|marker|> learned in the previous training stages. We train only this new embedding, the span head, and the LoRA adapters, while keeping the original backbone weights and decision head frozen. Each requested field gets its own <|locate|> token.
The span head uses <|locate|> ’s representation together with the state-token representations to score where matching spans start and end, and which start-end pairs belong together. It also uses the <|locate|> token’s representation to predict field-specific thresholds for these scores. Selected spans are returned as character positions in the original text.
We train the span head with an adapted InfoNCE loss that pushes every gold span above the threshold, and the threshold above every other span. The loss has two terms: The first one pushes the scores of correct spans above the threshold and the wrong spans. The second term pushes the threshold above the scores of wrong spans. Fields with no answer get only the second term, which teaches the model to return an empty list.
We train on a mix of span extraction tasks, including named entity recognition, PII detection and extractive question answering. We vary the field descriptions from short labels to detailed instructions, so the model learns to follow the request rather than memorize a fixed label set.
Locate teaches the model a structurally different task, and we want to add it without losing what the model already does well. Merging the locate adapters into the backbone causes some regression on decision requests. To limit this, we are running investigations such as more replay data from earlier stages and auxiliary objectives that keep the model’s outputs on decision requests close to those of the original model. However, we find that merging is currently still not lossless, so we keep the adapters unmerged and activate them only for locate requests.
Evaluation
We evaluate Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 on external benchmarks from the Hugging Face Decision Index, Vals AI’s ClaimBench, and Artificial Analysis Decision Index.
Across these evaluations, our models demonstrate strong performance. Even though these leaderboards include privately held tasks, they can still be gamed through repeated submission and iterative tuning based on leaderboard feedback. To complement these leaderboards, we evaluate the models on an internal suite combining private production tasks with held-out evaluations drawn from public non-benchmark datasets. These evaluations provide an additional check on generalization beyond public benchmarks, helping us distinguish broader improvements from gains specific to familiar evaluation suites.
Internally, we built a suite of more than 200 tasks spanning various domains and tasks such as classification, scoring, reranking, and entity extraction. To honestly assess Decider’s real-world performance, all evaluations are performed zero-shot, without task-specific fine-tuning, giving us a clear signal of where to improve the model.
Query classification
At Perplexity, we use a multi-head classification system to process each user query. Each query is first passed through an embedding model that acts as a feature extractor. The resulting embedding is then fed into multiple separate classification heads, including both binary and multi-label classifiers. For example, one head determines whether a user query should trigger web search.
Across 63 classification tasks with independently relabeled references by a frontier LLM, Decider v1.3 achieves 91.6% mean accuracy, exceeding our production classifiers by 6.54 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 also outperforms the production baseline, while Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14.
Domain-specific classification
We assembled a domain-specific evaluation suite from public datasets to assess decision models’ classification performance across seven domains: claim verification (6 tasks), healthcare (7), cybersecurity (8), programming (16), government (7), law (9) and finance (9).
For example, “judge the time complexity of a Python program”, or “use an annual financial report to determine whether a company’s unrestricted cash covers debt principal due within the next twelve months”. Decider v1.3 leads across all seven domains, outperforming Jev 1.14 by up to 12.9 percentage points in finance and 9.3 points in law. Decider Flash v1.3 trails Jev 1.14 in finance, programming, and law, and performs similarly in other domains.
Retrieval and Reranking
Search is at the core of Perplexity. We maintain a broad suite of retrieval tasks to evaluate our models’ reranking performance. For each task, we first use a pool of embedding models to retrieve the top 50 candidate documents from each corpus. We then rerank these candidates using Decider and compare its performance against a strong reranker baseline, Qwen3-Reranker-8B.
We evaluate Decider in a zero-shot, pointwise setting, using the model to directly score each query–document pair independently and rank documents by relevance. Across 72 retrieval tasks, Decider v1.3 achieves a mean nDCG@10 of 83.99, outperforming Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 1.81 points and Jev 1.14 by 2.24 points.
On the BEIR benchmark, both models outperform Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 8.78 and 7.05 nDCG@10 respectively. Against Jev 1.14, Decider v1.3 is 1.33 points higher, while the Flash version scores 0.4 lower.
Multilingual classification
To evaluate decision models beyond English, we assembled a multilingual classification benchmark comprising 19 language-specific tasks from 8 public datasets, with 46,484 examples across eight languages: German, Spanish, French, Italian, Russian, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese. The benchmark covers intent detection, topic classification, sentiment analysis, natural language inference, paraphrase detection, offensive language detection, and grammatical acceptability.
We report mean accuracy across tasks within each language, weighting each task equally. Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14 in all eight languages and Decider Flash v1.3 does so in six, with mean task accuracies of 88.16% for Decider v1.3 and 86.50% for Decider Flash v1.3, compared with 85.41% for Jev 1.14.
NER, PII and Extractive QA
We evaluate the locate feature on 17 out-of-domain tasks that test its extraction across various domains, input formats (text, tables, structured documents) and instructions (short labels, questions and detailed descriptions). The domains range from Wikipedia to scientific papers, cyber-threat reports, technical support, privacy policies, resumes, and legal contracts. The requests range from short label names such as “person” or “email address”, through questions about a table or a support ticket, to detailed field descriptions for structured extraction, such as the parties of an NDA or the total on an invoice.
We evaluate NER and PII using exact-span F1, which requires predicted spans to match the reference boundaries exactly. Extractive QA uses character-level F1, giving partial credit for overlapping answer text, while structured extraction uses field accuracy, the proportion of fields extracted correctly. For CV parsing, we average the NER and PII exact-span F1 scores.
We compare our models against general-purpose extraction models of different sizes: GLiNER large v2.5 (0.5B), Liquid d1 (2B) and Cloudflare’s Clairic (undisclosed). Decider v1.3 reaches an average score of 69.0 (using each task’s primary metric) and Decider Flash v1.3 reaches 63.6, compared with 43.3 for Liquid d1, 41.5 for Clairic and 33.6 for GLiNER large v2.5. Both Decider models lead in every category.
Image classification
Decider has natively supported vision tasks since v1. To evaluate its performance beyond text, we assembled a five-task benchmark suite with a particular focus on document classification, including invoices, letters, and resumes. The suite also covers satellite image classification, texture classification, pet breed classification, and animal counting.
Decider v1.3 achieves a mean accuracy of 76.99% across the five visual tasks, outperforming Jev 1.14 by 1.47 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 achieves 72.77%, demonstrating visual classification capabilities in a smaller model.
Real-world decision requests
We sampled one million deduplicated, PII-masked requests submitted to the Perplexity Decision API during its first 18 days of availability. Because each request can contain multiple questions about the same state, the sample comprises 2,318,887 individual questions. All requests were included with explicit user permission for research.
Production requests do not come with ground-truth labels, so we use frontier LLM judges to generate reference answers and measure each model’s agreement with them. We also group the requests into 10 task categories, including information extraction, domain classification, sentiment analysis, intent and routing, relevance ranking, content moderation, quality and compliance review, entity matching, business analysis, and an “Other” category. This breakdown shows how performance varies across real-world use cases.
The task mix is uneven: information extraction accounts for 425,402 questions, domain classification for 409,564, and sentiment analysis for 344,158. Together, these three categories make up 50.8% of the sampled questions.
Decider v1.3 achieves the highest agreement with the judges at 93.98%, compared with 93.68% for Decider v1.2 and 93.35% for Jev 1.14. Decider v1.3 and Jev 1.14 are closely matched on domain classification and sentiment analysis, with gaps of 0.34 and 0.07 percentage points, respectively. Jev leads by 0.69 points on relevance ranking, while Decider v1.3 leads by 0.93 points on information extraction (the most common task in the sample) and by 1.21 points on intent and routing.
The chart below compares the reported cost of running the same one million production requests. Each request can contain multiple questions, so the unit here is requests, not individual questions.
Robustness
We evaluated label sensitivity on 372 multiple-choice questions, making 4,788 requests per model. We reordered options, reassigned labels to answer texts, and renamed labels while preserving each question’s meaning, then checked whether the model’s semantic answer changed. Lower flip rates indicate greater stability.
Decider v1.3 changed its answer on just 0.27% of questions under each transformation, compared with 2.69–4.84% for Jev 1.14. We also repeated identical inputs to measure serving variability: Decider v1.3 showed no changes, while Jev 1.14 changed on 1.88% of questions.
How we use Decider
Decider is built for workflows that need fast and structured decisions. In this section we explore how to leverage them to produce meaningful impact on the way we work. Here are some that stood out.
Self-improving security rules
Internally, we are already using Decider to improve our security policies.
The activity of our agents is recorded and a series of rule-based checks are performed to identify any problematic behavior. A rule-based approach means that we can monitor our agents in real-time with negligible latency added. Offline, we use Decider to look at samples from these recorded agent logs. In the case that no problematic behavior was flagged, Decider checks if there is something that our set of rules missed; and in the case that an alarm was raised, Decider checks whether this was a false alarm. Any records where our rule set fails in either case are sent to an agent for triage and a fix to the rules is proposed, to be approved by a member of our security team.
In one day, Decider read 1 billion tokens across 7,000 agent sessions and identified flaws that led to 14 rule fixes, 6 of which were approved and shipped within two days. Replayed on a week of logs, the fixes cut our busiest rule's volume by 52%, and the widened rules caught about 40% more legitimate actions to investigate.
Monitoring RL rollouts
When we post-train models with reinforcement learning, aggregate metrics such as a terminal reward do not explain why a rollout (an individual attempt at a task) succeeded or failed. It can lose reward unfairly because a tool service or the sandbox failed, or receive undeserved reward if the evaluator overlooks an unsupported claim, such as a made-up value that no tool returned.
We use Decider to monitor rollouts for these cases. Code first identifies parts of a rollout that warrant closer inspection: a failed tool call and the surrounding reasoning, code that ran without errors, or the final answer. Decider then answers multiple-choice questions about each part, such as what failed in a step (a tool service, an external site, the sandbox, the harness, or the agent’s own code) and whether the agent interpreted the result correctly. We bundle all questions about a given part into a single request and store the probabilities rather than a verdict, so we can adjust thresholds later without querying Decider again. The monitor only observes and diagnoses: it never changes a reward or stops a run.
Page quality filtering
When crawling web pages to index and serve to users, many pages are too low quality to be of any use. This includes anti-bot walls, CAPTCHAs, and error pages, as well as correctly loaded web pages that just don’t contain any helpful information, such as spam, SEO filler or navigation-only pages. These low-quality pages need to be identified and filtered out of our index.
Using Decider, we can judge the quality of pages as we crawl them. In the same forward pass, we perform a suite of other classification tasks such as identifying the domain and intended audience of the content and whether it contains harmful, illegal, or personally identifiable information. Compared to using an LLM judge, Decider is considerably faster and cheaper.
Beyond these internal uses, Decider also fits workflows such as the following.
Visual QA
Because Decider reads images, it also works as a visual checker, reviewing style changes to web pages or apps and identifying faults. It can review page screenshots for clipped text, overlapping elements, broken layouts before a change ships, or flag charts whose design could mislead a reader or break a brand guide.
Browser navigation
Agents can use Decider for the small decisions inside larger tasks. A browser agent can send a screenshot at each step and receive detailed information about the state of the page and the expected outcome of each possible action.
Planning research tasks
Users’ questions can greatly vary in their complexity, as does the depth of search that needs to be performed to find an answer. Decider can estimate this before search begins, allowing for fewer resources to be spent on simple questions.
Getting started
Decider returns probabilities. The appropriate decision threshold depends on the application. Label frequencies and the relative costs of false positives and false negatives vary across use cases. We therefore encourage users to tune thresholds on a small, representative labeled development set rather than assume that a fixed cutoff will work equally well across tasks.
We recommend using Decider v1.3 for nuanced judgments, detailed rubrics, and workflows where errors are costly. Choose Decider Flash v1.3 for high-volume routing, labeling, and filtering where latency and cost are the main constraints. Evaluate both models on representative examples from your workload, then choose the model that meets your quality, latency, and budget requirements.
Both models are available as downloadable weights on Hugging Face under Apache license, through OpenRouter, and the Perplexity Decisions API.

articles.title: Perplexity Decider v1.3: Training, eval, and use cases
articles.body:
Perplexity Decider
How we train, evaluate, and use it.
We are releasing Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, the successors to our earlier decision models: v1, v1.1, v1.2, and Flash v1.2.
Decider Flash v1.3 is a smaller model distilled from Decider v1.3. Both models are available on Hugging Face under Apache license, through OpenRouter, and the Perplexity Decisions API.
Perplexity Decider is inspired by Jev, TypeSafe AI’s System One Model. It supports binary and multi-class classification with ordered or unordered labels, returning probabilities that applications can use to classify, route, rank, and evaluate inputs.
Both v1.3 models improve performance and robustness across a broad range of text and vision tasks through bidirectional attention, better-curated training data, and a refined training recipe. We also introduce locate, a new feature to highlight the selected content for named entity recognition, personal information identification, and extractive question-answering tasks.
In this post, we explain how we train and evaluate Decider and share how we use it internally at Perplexity.
What is a decision model?
A decision model is a general-purpose classifier. You give it an input and a set of questions each with its possible answers. For each question, it returns a probability distribution over the answers. It supports 3 question types:
- Yes / No: binary decisions.
- Multiple choice: custom multi-class labels.
- Score: ordered levels.
Decision models support a wide range of classification and scoring tasks:
- Judging outputs: assessing faithfulness, quality, and safety.
- Routing: directing requests to smaller or larger models based on difficulty.
- Moderation and security: detecting harmful content, phishing, and prompt injection in tool outputs.
- Filtering and tagging: organizing large collections of content.
- Retrieval and reranking: scoring search results by relevance.
Many of these tasks were previously handled by generative models like LLMs, even though they do not require free-form text generation. Decision models sit between LLMs and task-specific classifiers. They return probabilities for multiple questions about the same input in a single forward pass, avoiding token-by-token answer generation and sharing computation across questions. Unlike task-specific classifiers, they can handle new tasks through natural language prompts, a flexibility learned from training across diverse tasks in a shared question-answering format.
Training
Turning a generative LLM into a decision model
We build Decider by adapting strong generative LLM backbones. To explain the adaptation, we first describe how a request is represented. As illustrated below, a request consists out of a shared context (the state) and a number of questions. The state will be reused by all questions.
For example, given a document and its summary, a single request can ask whether the summary faithfully represents the document and whether it is intended for an expert or a general audience. After the state, each question block contains a question and its possible answers, each assigned a predefined label token such as A, B, or C. A special <|marker|> token indicates where to read out the model’s prediction. At this position, a learned linear output layer (a decision head), maps the hidden state to scores for the question’s answer options, which are then converted to probabilities.
We initialize the output layer from the base model, which normally scores next-token from the entire vocabulary, and only keep the rows corresponding to the predefined option tokens such as A, B, or C. This pruned layer is then trained to turn the hidden state of  <|marker|> into answer scores. This approach covers all classification questions because they can all be formulated as a multiple choice.
For training, we take hundreds of public datasets spanning diverse tasks (sentiment, natural language inference, intent detection, entity matching, moderation, fact checking, ratings, etc.) and convert each example into the unified format described above: a state, one or more questions, their options and a target. The target can be the single correct option if we have gold labels, or a probability distribution over options.
In v1.3, we introduce locate, which extracts text from the state instead of selecting from predefined options. A locate question describes what to find, using either a short label such as “location” or an instruction such as “Extract the city name where the job is located.” The model returns the exact matching text from the state, along with its start and end character locations. If it identifies no matches, it returns an empty list.
Because of shared state, a single request can combine locate, classification, and scoring questions about the same input. For example, it can ask whether a job requires senior-level experience and extract the required skills.
Bidirectional attention: letting the model read both ways
Our models start from strong pretrained generative backbones, whose causal attention lets each token attend only to itself and preceding tokens. Our ablation studies showed that making the backbone’s full-attention layers bidirectional improves performance, so we adopt this design to let each token incorporate context from the entire input.
Bidirectional attention introduces another design choice: how should the state and questions interact? We considered three attention patterns, with different implications for performance, answer stability, and cache reuse:
- Everything sees everything (v1.2): The state and all questions are processed together with full bidirectional attention. Computation over the state is shared, but an answer to one question can change depending on what else is asked.
- Isolated questions (v1.3): The state attends to all the questions, while each question attends only to the state and its own tokens. Questions can still influence one another indirectly through the shared state but results are more stable.
- Fully cacheable: The state only attends to itself, while each question attends to the state and its own tokens. The state is question-independent and reusable across requests to take advantage of prompt caching. We don't use it by default, because letting the state see the questions matters a lot for several tasks, but a small fine-tuning can switch a model to it.
We ultimately chose isolated questions for their strong performance and stability.
Training recipe
Training proceeds in three stages for both model sizes. We first train the larger model, based on Qwen3.8-27B, using cross-entropy on large datasets, then distill it into the smaller Qwen3.5-4B model.
The first stage is generalist training, where we fully fine-tune the model on large-scale corpora. In this stage, we only accept data that helps the model across the board and is not specific to any benchmark; we thus exclude any benchmark training splits.
After this generalist model is trained, we run a second, more fine-grained stage using LoRA. The data used in this stage is targeted toward specific domains and tasks. We add data in the second stage rather than the first one if we observe narrow gains or if we observe some regressions on other tasks. We use LoRA to avoid drifting too much from the generalist model and risking losing performance to fit those specific domains. The goal is to improve performance while retaining the backbone’s general knowledge. We also use a weight when merging the LoRA back into the base model, to control the drift more precisely and favor held-out metrics above any in-domain gains.
Finally, we add a vision-specific step. Similar to the second stage, the vision step is treated as another fine-grained specialization step, using a LoRA adapter that is merged back to the base model with a weight. Some vision capabilities can come at the price of text performance. Since we observe much more usage of the models on text, we prioritize text metrics over vision metrics.
For both text stages, we use the average weights from three runs, each using a different random seed. We found this improves the performance and robustness of the aggregated model.
Once the final large model is obtained, we apply the same three-stage training procedure to the smaller model. Here, the large model acts as the teacher: its predicted output distribution replaces the gold labels, and the smaller model is trained to minimize the KL divergence between its predictions and those of the teacher. This distillation objective outperforms cross-entropy on the same training data. While cross-entropy performs better on benchmarks with dedicated training data, it generalizes less well to held-out data. We hypothesize that distillation better transfers the teacher’s output distribution, including its confidence over non-gold alternatives, whereas cross-entropy encourages overfitting to the benchmark-specific training distribution. We therefore adopt the KL-based distillation objective.
To mitigate train-test contamination, we remove any training samples that could overlap with any evaluation we use. This is important because some public training datasets contain large parts of some evaluation datasets. We also conduct extensive bias audits and removal to make sure our gains are reliable and not just driven by learned biases.
Adding the ability to extract information
The locate feature extracts information such as named entities from text, without changing how it answers ordinary requests. To do so, we introduce an additional training stage: we add a new special token, <|locate|>, a span head, and LoRA adapter to Decider. 
We initialize  <|locate|> ’s embedding from <|marker|> learned in the previous training stages. We train only this new embedding, the span head, and the LoRA adapters, while keeping the original backbone weights and decision head frozen. Each requested field gets its own <|locate|> token.
The span head uses <|locate|> ’s representation together with the state-token representations to score where matching spans start and end, and which start-end pairs belong together. It also uses the <|locate|> token’s representation to predict field-specific thresholds for these scores. Selected spans are returned as character positions in the original text.
We train the span head with an adapted InfoNCE loss that pushes every gold span above the threshold, and the threshold above every other span. The loss has two terms: The first one pushes the scores of correct spans above the threshold and the wrong spans. The second term pushes the threshold above the scores of wrong spans. Fields with no answer get only the second term, which teaches the model to return an empty list.
We train on a mix of span extraction tasks, including named entity recognition, PII detection and extractive question answering. We vary the field descriptions from short labels to detailed instructions, so the model learns to follow the request rather than memorize a fixed label set.
Locate teaches the model a structurally different task, and we want to add it without losing what the model already does well. Merging the locate adapters into the backbone causes some regression on decision requests. To limit this, we are running investigations such as more replay data from earlier stages and auxiliary objectives that keep the model’s outputs on decision requests close to those of the original model. However, we find that merging is currently still not lossless, so we keep the adapters unmerged and activate them only for locate requests.
Evaluation
We evaluate Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 on external benchmarks from the Hugging Face Decision Index, Vals AI’s ClaimBench, and Artificial Analysis Decision Index.
Across these evaluations, our models demonstrate strong performance. Even though these leaderboards include privately held tasks, they can still be gamed through repeated submission and iterative tuning based on leaderboard feedback. To complement these leaderboards, we evaluate the models on an internal suite combining private production tasks with held-out evaluations drawn from public non-benchmark datasets. These evaluations provide an additional check on generalization beyond public benchmarks, helping us distinguish broader improvements from gains specific to familiar evaluation suites.
Internally, we built a suite of more than 200 tasks spanning various domains and tasks such as classification, scoring, reranking, and entity extraction. To honestly assess Decider’s real-world performance, all evaluations are performed zero-shot, without task-specific fine-tuning, giving us a clear signal of where to improve the model.
Query classification
At Perplexity, we use a multi-head classification system to process each user query. Each query is first passed through an embedding model that acts as a feature extractor. The resulting embedding is then fed into multiple separate classification heads, including both binary and multi-label classifiers. For example, one head determines whether a user query should trigger web search.
Across 63 classification tasks with independently relabeled references by a frontier LLM, Decider v1.3 achieves 91.6% mean accuracy, exceeding our production classifiers by 6.54 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 also outperforms the production baseline, while Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14.
Domain-specific classification
We assembled a domain-specific evaluation suite from public datasets to assess decision models’ classification performance across seven domains: claim verification (6 tasks), healthcare (7), cybersecurity (8), programming (16), government (7), law (9) and finance (9).
For example, “judge the time complexity of a Python program”, or “use an annual financial report to determine whether a company’s unrestricted cash covers debt principal due within the next twelve months”. Decider v1.3 leads across all seven domains, outperforming Jev 1.14 by up to 12.9 percentage points in finance and 9.3 points in law. Decider Flash v1.3 trails Jev 1.14 in finance, programming, and law, and performs similarly in other domains.
Retrieval and Reranking
Search is at the core of Perplexity. We maintain a broad suite of retrieval tasks to evaluate our models’ reranking performance. For each task, we first use a pool of embedding models to retrieve the top 50 candidate documents from each corpus. We then rerank these candidates using Decider and compare its performance against a strong reranker baseline, Qwen3-Reranker-8B.
We evaluate Decider in a zero-shot, pointwise setting, using the model to directly score each query–document pair independently and rank documents by relevance. Across 72 retrieval tasks, Decider v1.3 achieves a mean nDCG@10 of 83.99, outperforming Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 1.81 points and Jev 1.14 by 2.24 points.
On the BEIR benchmark, both models outperform Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 8.78 and 7.05 nDCG@10 respectively. Against Jev 1.14, Decider v1.3 is 1.33 points higher, while the Flash version scores 0.4 lower.
Multilingual classification
To evaluate decision models beyond English, we assembled a multilingual classification benchmark comprising 19 language-specific tasks from 8 public datasets, with 46,484 examples across eight languages: German, Spanish, French, Italian, Russian, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese. The benchmark covers intent detection, topic classification, sentiment analysis, natural language inference, paraphrase detection, offensive language detection, and grammatical acceptability.
We report mean accuracy across tasks within each language, weighting each task equally. Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14 in all eight languages and Decider Flash v1.3 does so in six, with mean task accuracies of 88.16% for Decider v1.3 and 86.50% for Decider Flash v1.3, compared with 85.41% for Jev 1.14.
NER, PII and Extractive QA
We evaluate the locate feature on 17 out-of-domain tasks that test its extraction across various domains, input formats (text, tables, structured documents) and instructions (short labels, questions and detailed descriptions). The domains range from Wikipedia to scientific papers, cyber-threat reports, technical support, privacy policies, resumes, and legal contracts. The requests range from short label names such as “person” or “email address”, through questions about a table or a support ticket, to detailed field descriptions for structured extraction, such as the parties of an NDA or the total on an invoice.
We evaluate NER and PII using exact-span F1, which requires predicted spans to match the reference boundaries exactly. Extractive QA uses character-level F1, giving partial credit for overlapping answer text, while structured extraction uses field accuracy, the proportion of fields extracted correctly. For CV parsing, we average the NER and PII exact-span F1 scores.
We compare our models against general-purpose extraction models of different sizes: GLiNER large v2.5 (0.5B), Liquid d1 (2B) and Cloudflare’s Clairic (undisclosed). Decider v1.3 reaches an average score of 69.0 (using each task’s primary metric) and Decider Flash v1.3 reaches 63.6, compared with 43.3 for Liquid d1, 41.5 for Clairic and 33.6 for GLiNER large v2.5. Both Decider models lead in every category.
Image classification
Decider has natively supported vision tasks since v1. To evaluate its performance beyond text, we assembled a five-task benchmark suite with a particular focus on document classification, including invoices, letters, and resumes. The suite also covers satellite image classification, texture classification, pet breed classification, and animal counting.
Decider v1.3 achieves a mean accuracy of 76.99% across the five visual tasks, outperforming Jev 1.14 by 1.47 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 achieves 72.77%, demonstrating visual classification capabilities in a smaller model.
Real-world decision requests

Because each request can contain multiple questions about the same state, the sample comprises 2,318,887 individual questions. All requests were included with explicit user permission for research.
