articles.title: $11.4M in Nvidia hardware vanishes during shipment from CA to TX
articles.body:
Six pallets of NVIDIA computer hardware worth a reported $11.4 million disappeared during a shipment from California to Texas. A truck collected the merchandise in Oakland on Aug. 29 for delivery to Fort Worth. Investigators reportedly tracked the vehicle through several extended stops before losing its trail in Southern California. The Oakland Police Department confirmed an ongoing grand theft investigation following a complaint filed Sept. 13, 2026. The disappearance comes amid reports of nearly $111 million in stolen data center freight involving other high-value technology shipments.
According to The Mercury News, the vehicle displayed a food transportation company’s logo during the scheduled pickup. The driver subsequently traveled south, making several stops lasting multiple hours. Investigators eventually lost track of the truck in San Bernardino County. A separate $12 million cargo theft investigation involved suspects who allegedly exploited established trucking identities to obtain freight. Authorities have not linked the two investigations.
Oakland police confirm investigation
The Oakland Police Department provided FreightWaves with the following statement:
“The Oakland Police Department (OPD) is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026. The investigation is ongoing, and anyone with information is asked to contact the OPD General Crimes Unit at (510) 238-3728.”
The Sept. 13 complaint date does not establish when the theft occurred. Police have not confirmed the reported $11.4 million valuation or identified the specific merchandise. Authorities also have not identified the cargo’s owner, shipper, motor carrier or driver. Investigators have not publicly explained the vehicle’s extended stops or established whether criminals impersonated a transportation provider. Police have not announced arrests or confirmed any recovery of the merchandise. FreightWaves contacted NVIDIA for comment and followed up, but the company has not responded.
Previous thefts involving NVIDIA products
The Oakland investigation follows other significant thefts involving NVIDIA merchandise in Northern California. During 2025, Fremont and Union City police investigated burglaries involving more than $7.5 million in NVIDIA products. Those incidents targeted valuable computer hardware at separate locations. Authorities have not established any connection between those investigations and the latest disappearance.
In a separate September incident, thieves stole two PlusAI trailers, including one displaying NVIDIA branding, from a Fremont, California, warehouse. The trailers contained approximately 40,000 pounds of sand rather than NVIDIA hardware. Police recovered both trailers in nearby Newark. Investigators have not established any connection between that theft and the Oakland case.
Why it matters
The reported disappearance of $11.4 million in NVIDIA hardware underscores the financial stakes of transporting high-value freight. Regardless of how this shipment disappeared, carrier verification, shipment visibility and communication remain critical throughout transportation.
Click here for more articles on cargo theft and freight fraud by Phil Brink.

articles.title: Serving GLM-5.3 at 607.8 tok/s across two Nvidia DGX stations with vLLM
articles.body:
Running a frontier-scale model locally means keeping all its weights in GPU memory; the largest models no longer fit on one machine. Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve one model through a single endpoint, with tensor parallelism splitting the model weights and computation across both GPUs.
The NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model, a quantized version of Z.ai’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, has 753 billion parameters, with 40 billion activated per token. Sparse activation reduces computation, but all model weights still need to remain available because each token can be routed to different experts. At about 464 GB, the checkpoint exceeds the 252 GB of HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU. This tutorial uses two DGX Stations to keep the weights in GPU memory, with CPU weight offload disabled.
Before starting, connect the two Stations with the Connect Two DGX Stations playbook.
This post shows how to serve GLM-5.3 locally across two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM, send a request, and measure behavior under concurrent load. Tensor parallelism (TP=2) splits the model’s tensors across the two GB300 GPUs. Both Stations compute every request, and Station A returns the answer through one OpenAI-compatible API. By the end, you’ll have a working endpoint and a baseline for how it behaves under load.
Prerequisites
- Two GB300 DGX Stations running Linux, connected and validated with the Connect Two DGX Stations playbook, including its GPU-memory RDMA test on both rails.
- SSH and sudo access on both Stations with the same Linux username. Docker and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit come preinstalled with the DGX Station software stack. Allow outbound access to the container registry, Hugging Face, and package repositories.
- At least 464 GB of free disk space on each Station for its copy of the checkpoint, plus room for the vLLM container image and temporary files.
- Acceptance of the NVIDIA Open Model Agreement and the original GLM-5.3 license terms, listed on the model card. SPEED-Bench is governed by the NVIDIA Evaluation Dataset License Agreement.
- A Hugging Face account and read access token, with access to the gated cais/hle dataset: sign in, open its page, and select Agree and access repository. Step 5 downloads SPEED-Bench prompts from this dataset.
The companion video follows the same workflow.
Step 1. Prepare the two Stations
This tutorial uses a separate computer, such as your laptop, to manage both Stations. Start by opening an SSH session to each Station from that computer. Alternatively, work from a local terminal on each Station. Run every command in this step on both Stations unless it starts with “On A.”
The two Stations run the same container and checkpoint in different roles: Station A (rank 0) hosts the API, and Station B (rank 1) runs only a worker, with no API server.
First, check Docker access and collect the network values you’ll use later:
docker version
ibdev2netdev
ip -br addr
The ibdev2netdev output lists the two direct rails, cx8r0 and cx8r1. Pick one for serving traffic, for example cx8r1, and note two things for it on each Station:
- Its RDMA device, on the ibdev2netdev line that ends with the rail’s name. In mlx5_1 port 1 ==> cx8r1 (Up), the device is mlx5_1.
- Its IPv4 address, on the ip -br addr line that starts with the rail’s name. In cx8r1 UP 192.168.101.1/24, the address is 192.168.101.1.
The rail name and device are the same on both Stations; only the IPv4 address differs.
Next, create ~/glm53.env on each Station. This file stores the values that later commands use:
nano ~/glm53.env
Paste the following block and replace each <...> placeholder, keeping the quotes, with the values you noted.
RANK="<NODE_RANK>"                    # RANK="0" on Station A, RANK="1" on Station B 
HEAD_IP="<STATION_A_IPV4_ADDRESS>"    # IPv4 address you noted on Station A; same in both files
WORKER_IP="<STATION_B_IPV4_ADDRESS>"  # IPv4 address you noted on Station B; same in both files
RAIL_IFACE="<RAIL_NAME>"              # Rail you picked, for example cx8r1; same in both files
RAIL_HCA="<RDMA_DEVICE>"              # RDMA device you noted, for example mlx5_1; same in both files
IMG=vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0-aarch64
IMG+=@sha256:4864d46625cbc3307623e29ac742030655e27249feba7b97ec925ce4cc4dfb56
MODEL_REPO=nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4
MODEL_REV=e3b8f9f2fad29727dfa95e766c5cac18ea1414bf
MODEL_HOST="$HOME/models/GLM-5.3-NVFP4"
CONTAINER=glm53-full
PORT=8000
if [ "$RANK" = 0 ]; then
  NODE_IP=$HEAD_IP; PEER_IP=$WORKER_IP
else
  NODE_IP=$WORKER_IP; PEER_IP=$HEAD_IP
fi
GPU_UUID=$(nvidia-smi --query-gpu=uuid,name --format=csv,noheader |
  awk -F, '$2 ~ /GB300/ {gsub(/ /,"",$1); print $1; exit}')
For example, with the default addresses on cx8r1, Station A’s file starts like this. Station B’s file is identical except for RANK="1":
RANK="0"
HEAD_IP="192.168.101.1"
WORKER_IP="192.168.101.2"
RAIL_IFACE="cx8r1"
RAIL_HCA="mlx5_1"
MODEL_HOST is built from your home directory, and Step 2 copies the checkpoint over SSH to the same path on Station B. 
On both Stations, load the values and check storage, connectivity, and baseline memory:
source ~/glm53.env
mkdir -p "$MODEL_HOST" && df -h "$MODEL_HOST"
ethtool "$RAIL_IFACE"
ip link show dev "$RAIL_IFACE"
ping -I "$RAIL_IFACE" -M do -s 8972 -c 3 "$PEER_IP"
timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value
nvidia-smi
These checks catch cabling and addressing mistakes before they surface as NCCL timeouts. Expect a 400000Mb/s link, MTU 9000, successful jumbo-frame pings, and synchronized time. nvidia-smi should show no compute processes on the GB300. On a Station with a display GPU, Xorg can appear on both GPUs with a few MiB. 
Step 2 copies the checkpoint from A to B over SSH, so A needs passwordless access to B. On A, create a key without a passphrase (see SSH keys for details), copy its public key to B after checking B’s host fingerprint, and confirm the login:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
ssh-copy-id "$WORKER_IP"
ssh -o BatchMode=yes "$WORKER_IP" hostname
Step 2. Download and copy the model
Tensor parallelism requires both ranks to run the same software against the same weights. Start by pulling the pinned image on both Stations:
docker pull "$IMG" &&
docker image inspect "$IMG" --format '{{.Architecture}} {{.RepoDigests}}'
The pull can take several minutes. Matching arm64 digests mean both ranks run identical software.
On A, download the pinned checkpoint. At about 464 GB, it takes roughly an hour at 1 Gb/s, or about six minutes at 10 Gb/s:
mkdir -p "$MODEL_HOST"
docker run --rm --network host -v "$MODEL_HOST:/model" \
  --entrypoint bash "$IMG" -lc \
  "exec hf download '$MODEL_REPO' --revision '$MODEL_REV' --local-dir /model"
When hf download prints Downloaded, copy the files to B. On A:
ssh "$WORKER_IP" "mkdir -p '$MODEL_HOST'" &&
rsync -aH --info=progress2 --exclude '.cache/' \
  "$MODEL_HOST/" "$WORKER_IP:$MODEL_HOST/"
Each disk keeps the full checkpoint; vLLM partitions the weights across the GPUs at load time, with no further quantization.
On A, compare both copies (the check reads B’s file list over SSH), then validate the checkpoint:
(
  set -euo pipefail
  L=$(find "$MODEL_HOST" -path '*/.cache' -prune -o \
    -type f -printf '%P %s\n' | LC_ALL=C sort | sha256sum)
  R=$(ssh "$WORKER_IP" "set -o pipefail; find '$MODEL_HOST' \
    -path '*/.cache' -prune -o -type f -printf '%P %s\\n' | \
    LC_ALL=C sort | sha256sum")
  test "$L" = "$R"
  test "$(find "$MODEL_HOST" -maxdepth 1 \
    -name 'model-*-of-00050.safetensors' | wc -l)" = 50
  python3 -c "import json; c=json.load(open('$MODEL_HOST/config.json')); \
assert c['architectures']==['GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM']; \
assert c['quantization_config']['quant_algo']=='MIXED_PRECISION'"
  echo MODEL_READY
)
MODEL_READY means both Stations hold the same file names and sizes in the expected layout. MIXED_PRECISION is expected: NVFP4 quantization targets MoE-block linear weights and activations, not every tensor.
Step 3. Launch the distributed service
This step turns two machines into one service: the same launch script runs on both Stations, reads ~/glm53.env, and starts one vLLM rank on each. Two settings matter most if you adapt it: --max-model-len 98304, the context ceiling in tokens, which covers input plus output, and --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93, which gives vLLM 93% of GPU memory. If you change other flags, change one at a time and test again.
For the latest recommended configurations, see NVIDIA’s Local AI recipe repository.
On both Stations, create a file named ~/launch-glm53.sh:
nano ~/launch-glm53.sh
The script enables multi-token prediction (MTP), a form of speculative decoding: the model’s MTP layer drafts four tokens per step, and vLLM verifies them with the full model before accepting them, so each step can produce several tokens. The gain depends on how often drafts are accepted, which varies with the prompt.
FP8 KV-cache storage halves cache memory compared with 16-bit storage, leaving room for more tokens. Prefix caching is enabled to avoid reprocessing prompt prefixes the server has already seen. Paste the script below; it checks your configuration, finds the RoCE GID index for the selected rail, and starts this Station’s vLLM rank in a container:
set -euo pipefail
source "$HOME/glm53.env"
case "$RANK" in 0|1) ;; *) echo "Invalid RANK" >&2; exit 1;; esac
test -n "$GPU_UUID"
test -f "$MODEL_HOST/config.json"
GID_INDEX=$(/usr/sbin/show_gids 2>/dev/null |
  awk -v d="$RAIL_HCA" -v ip="$NODE_IP" \
  '$1==d && $5==ip && $6=="v2" {g=$3} END {if(g!="") print g}')
test -n "$GID_INDEX"
HEADLESS=
if [ "$RANK" = 1 ]; then HEADLESS=--headless; fi
SPEC_CONFIG='{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":4}'
KERNEL_CONFIG='{"enable_flashinfer_autotune":false,"moe_backend":"flashinfer_cutlass"}'
COMPILE_CONFIG='{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_DECODE_ONLY","cudagraph_capture_sizes":[5,10,20,40,80],"pass_config":{"fuse_allreduce_rms":false}}'
docker run -d --name "$CONTAINER" \
  --gpus device="$GPU_UUID" --network host --ipc host --shm-size 32g \
  --device /dev/infiniband --cap-add IPC_LOCK \
  --ulimit memlock=-1 --ulimit stack=67108864 \
  -v "$MODEL_HOST:/model:ro" \
  -e RANK="$RANK" -e HEADLESS="$HEADLESS" \
  -e MASTER_ADDR="$HEAD_IP" -e MODEL_REPO="$MODEL_REPO" -e PORT="$PORT" \
  -e SPEC_CONFIG="$SPEC_CONFIG" -e KERNEL_CONFIG="$KERNEL_CONFIG" \
  -e COMPILE_CONFIG="$COMPILE_CONFIG" \
  -e NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1 -e NCCL_IB_HCA="$RAIL_HCA" \
  -e NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX="$GID_INDEX" \
  -e NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT=22 -e NCCL_IB_RETRY_CNT=7 \
  -e VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_FLASHINFER=0 -e VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_SYMM_MEM=0 \
  -e NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME="$RAIL_IFACE" -e GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME="$RAIL_IFACE" \
  -e NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5 -e NCCL_DEBUG=INFO -e NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NET \
  -e NCCL_DEBUG_FILE='/tmp/nccl_%h_%p.log' -e VLLM_HOST_IP="$NODE_IP" \
  -e VLLM_EXECUTE_MODEL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1800 \
  -e PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True \
  -e VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 -e FLASHINFER_DISABLE_VERSION_CHECK=1 \
  --entrypoint bash "$IMG" -lc '
    set -euo pipefail  
    # Use NCCL 2.30.7 from the image: older versions can deadlock
    # cross-node CUDA graph replays over RoCE (vLLM issue #52504).
    export VLLM_NCCL_SO_PATH=$(python3 -c "import nvidia.nccl,os;
print(os.path.join(list(nvidia.nccl.__path__)[0], \"lib\", \"libnccl.so.2\"))")
    test -f "$VLLM_NCCL_SO_PATH"
    EXTRA=()
    if [ -n "$HEADLESS" ]; then EXTRA+=("$HEADLESS"); fi
    exec vllm serve /model --served-model-name "$MODEL_REPO" \
      --host 0.0.0.0 --port "$PORT" \
      --nnodes 2 --node-rank "$RANK" --master-addr "$MASTER_ADDR" \
      --master-port 29501 --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
      --speculative-config "$SPEC_CONFIG" \
      --max-model-len 98304  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
      --block-size 128 --max-num-seqs 16 \
      --trust-remote-code --disable-custom-all-reduce \
      --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --enable-prefix-caching \
      --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93 \
      --enable-prompt-tokens-details \
      --kernel-config "$KERNEL_CONFIG" --compilation-config "$COMPILE_CONFIG" \
      --distributed-timeout-seconds 1800 \
      --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser glm47 --reasoning-parser glm47 \
      "${EXTRA[@]}"
  '
Run the script on B first, then on A:
bash ~/launch-glm53.sh
Each command prints a container ID and returns immediately; the service is not ready yet. B’s worker waits for A to join, then each Station loads its share of the weights from local storage, prepares kernels, and captures CUDA graphs. This takes several minutes.
On A, follow the log to see when the service is ready (--since hides output from earlier runs):
docker logs --follow --since "$(docker inspect \
  --format '{{.State.StartedAt}}' "$CONTAINER")" "$CONTAINER"
When the log shows Application startup complete, press Ctrl+C to stop following it; the service keeps running. 
At this point one model spans two machines. Neither GPU holds a complete copy, and neither can answer a request alone: every token needs both ranks to exchange partial results over the RoCE rail.
The remaining GPU memory holds the KV cache, which stores the context of in-flight requests. The startup log reports its capacity (GPU KV cache size). All requests in flight share it, so longer prompts or more users need more of it. If you run out, lower --max-model-len or send fewer requests at once.
Step 4. Verify serving and send a request
On A, check the API (127.0.0.1 is A itself):
docker exec "$CONTAINER" curl -fsS --max-time 10 \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/health" >/dev/null && echo HEALTH_OK
HEALTH_OK proves that Station A answers. Next, on both Stations, check that the ranks communicate over GPU RDMA rather than falling back to TCP sockets. The check reads the NCCL logs that the launcher writes through NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, and the same block shows the loaded memory:
docker exec "$CONTAINER" bash -lc '
  set -euo pipefail
  files=(/tmp/nccl_*.log)
  test -e "${files[0]}"
  grep -hE "NET/IB.*GDRDMA|GPU Direct RDMA Enabled" "${files[@]}" >/dev/null
  grep -hF "$NCCL_IB_HCA" "${files[@]}" >/dev/null
  if grep -hE "NET/Socket|NCCL WARN|NCCL ERROR" "${files[@]}"; then
    exit 1
  fi
  echo RDMA_CHECK_OK
'
nvidia-smi
RDMA_CHECK_OK means the check passed with no warnings. In nvidia-smi, A shows the VLLM::Worker_TP0 process and B shows VLLM::Worker_TP1, one rank per GPU. The startup log reports about 218 GiB of weights per GPU, roughly half the checkpoint, which confirms that the model is split across the two GPUs.
On A, send a chat request through the OpenAI-compatible API:
docker exec "$CONTAINER" curl -fsS --max-time 120 \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4",
    "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Quarterly units sold: Q1 = 120; Q2 = 180; Q3 = 150. Summarize the trend in one sentence and calculate the percentage change from Q1 to Q2."}],
    "temperature":0,"max_tokens":4096,
    "chat_template_kwargs":{"reasoning_effort":"low"}}' |
python3 -c 'import json,sys; c=json.load(sys.stdin)["choices"][0];
print(c["message"]["content"]); print("finish_reason:",c["finish_reason"])'
The response should look like this:
**Trend:** Units sold rose sharply in Q2 before partially declining in Q3, remaining above the Q1 level.
**Q1 → Q2 percentage change:** (180 - 120) / 120 × 100 = **50% increase**
finish_reason: stop
finish_reason: stop means the model finished its answer instead of hitting the token limit. The request sets reasoning_effort to low in chat_template_kwargs. GLM-5.3 also accepts high and max, which let it reason longer before answering, at the cost of latency. Because the launcher enables tool calling (--enable-auto-tool-choice), agent frameworks that use the OpenAI tools API can call the same endpoint.
Step 5. Concurrency and release resources
AIPerf, the NVIDIA benchmarking tool for inference endpoints, measures throughput and latency. Installing it inside the serving container can change vLLM’s dependencies, so on A, install it in its own virtual environment:
sudo apt update &&
sudo apt install -y python3.12-venv python3.12-dev build-essential &&
python3.12 -m venv "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0" &&
"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/pip" install 'aiperf==0.12.0' &&
"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/pip" check
The install should end with No broken requirements found.
AIPerf can send synthetic prompts or replay an existing dataset. This tutorial uses the 80 Coding conversations from SPEED-Bench, a set of real prompts built to evaluate speculative decoding, so MTP is measured on realistic text. SPEED-Bench’s preparation script fetches these prompts from several Hugging Face datasets, including the gated cais/hle: if you haven’t already, open its page and select Agree and access repository before you continue. Then, on A, log in to Hugging Face:
"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/hf" auth login
Next, download and prepare the dataset. See the official AIPerf guide for details:
SPEED_BENCH_DIR="$HOME/datasets/speed-bench"
mkdir -p "$SPEED_BENCH_DIR"
curl -fLsS https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Skills/refs/heads/main/nemo_skills/dataset/speed-bench/prepare.py | \
  "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/python" - --config qualitative --output_dir "$SPEED_BENCH_DIR"
On A, check the dataset and service. Continue when the check prints BENCHMARK_READY:
(
  set -euo pipefail
  source ~/glm53.env
  curl -fsS "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT/health" >/dev/null
  "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/python" - <<'PY_CHECK'
import json
from pathlib import Path
root = Path.home()
path = root / "datasets/speed-bench/qualitative.jsonl"
assert path.exists(), "Dataset missing: rerun the SPEED-Bench preparation"
rows = [json.loads(line) for line in path.read_text().splitlines() if line.strip()]
coding = [row for row in rows if row["category"] == "coding"]
assert len(coding) == 80, "Expected 80 Coding conversations"
assert sum(len(row["messages"]) for row in coding) == 89
assert all("FULL BENCHMARK DATA SHOULD BE FETCHED" not in message["content"]
           for row in coding for message in row["messages"])
print("BENCHMARK_READY: dataset has 80 Coding conversations, 89 turns in total.")
PY_CHECK
)
The full sweep covers concurrency 1, 8, 16, and 32. At each level, AIPerf sends 3×C warmup requests, then measures 10×C requests, where C is the concurrency. Some conversations are sent more than once at higher concurrency.
Benchmark requests use the model’s default reasoning effort (max) and an 8,192-token output cap; responses can finish before reaching it. Full sweeps can take several hours.
 A two-hour request timeout leaves room for long responses, --server-metrics collects server counters used to measure MTP acceptance, and --export-level raw keeps each response for inspection. 
For a quick test, run the block below on A with both containers running and no other API traffic. It tests C1 and C8 with prefix caching enabled, as in the reference measurements in Table 2, below.
(
  set -euo pipefail
  source ~/glm53.env
  CODING_DATASET="$HOME/datasets/speed-bench/qualitative.jsonl"
  test -f "$CODING_DATASET"
 export CONCURRENCIES=${CONCURRENCIES:-"1 8"} # Quick run: C1 and C8.
  # Optional full benchmark: follow the reproduction instructions below.
  # Step 3: --max-num-seqs 16 -> export CONCURRENCIES="1 8 16"
  # Step 3: --max-num-seqs 32 -> export CONCURRENCIES=32
  RUN_DIR="$HOME/aiperf-results/blog-coding-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
  for C in $CONCURRENCIES;  do
    ART="$RUN_DIR/c$C"
    env -u HF_HUB_OFFLINE -u TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE \
      "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/aiperf" profile \
      -m "$MODEL_REPO" --url "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT" \
      --endpoint-type chat --streaming --tokenizer "$MODEL_HOST" \
      --custom-dataset-type speed_bench_coding --input-file "$CODING_DATASET" \
      --request-count "$((10 * C))" --warmup-request-count "$((3 * C))" \
      --osl 8192 \
      --use-server-token-count --concurrency "$C" --random-seed 42 \
      --request-timeout-seconds 7200 \
      --server-metrics "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT/metrics" \
      --export-level raw --artifact-dir "$ART"
    printf "Results: %s\n" "$ART"
  done
  printf "Results directory: %s\n" "$RUN_DIR"
)
AIPerf saves metrics, raw responses, and logs in the results directory. Warmup requests are excluded from the reported metrics.
Optional: Reproduce Table 2. In ~/launch-glm53.sh from Step 3 on both Stations, keep --enable-prefix-caching and set --max-num-seqs to 16 or 32 for the corresponding group shown in the comments above. Before each group, stop and remove the current containers on A, then B (docker stop --timeout 60 "$CONTAINER", followed by docker rm "$CONTAINER"). Relaunch the updated script on B, then A with bash ~/launch-glm53.sh and wait for Application startup complete. On A, run the matching export CONCURRENCIES command from the comments, then rerun the AIPerf block.
To test without prefix caching, replace --enable-prefix-caching with --no-enable-prefix-caching in the Step 3 script on both Stations, then recreate the containers as above. Performance may differ from Table 2.
Figure 2 compares overall output throughput across measured requests with mean per-user throughput. Token counts include reasoning.
Table 2, below, shows how throughput and latency change as more requests share the service.
Overall throughput peaks at 607.8 tok/s at C16. It falls to 385.0 tok/s at C32, where mean request latency is 453.5 s. Higher concurrency also reduces mean per-user throughput, from 115.3 tok/s at C1 to 13.0 tok/s at C32.
After the requests finish, stop the vLLM container on A, then on B:
docker stop --timeout 60 "$CONTAINER"
docker inspect --format \
  'Status={{.State.Status}} Running={{.State.Running}}' "$CONTAINER"
nvidia-smi
The status should read Status=exited Running=false, with no vLLM processes in nvidia-smi; the checkpoint, containers, and results stay on disk. To resume, run docker start "$CONTAINER" on B, then A, and repeat the Step 4 checks.
Troubleshoot common blockers
- Missing variables or SSH failure: source ~/glm53.env after reconnecting; verify A-to-B key authentication and B’s fingerprint.
- SPEED-Bench preparation fails with a gated-dataset error: sign in to Hugging Face with the same account, open the cais/hle page, select Agree and access repository, then rerun the preparation.
- Startup or RDMA check failure: inspect docker logs "$CONTAINER" on both nodes; verify the checkpoint and the GID, and rerun the playbook’s validation (script 07).
- CUDA out of memory: lower --max-model-len or concurrency, then retest.
Put the endpoint to work
You now have a 753-billion-parameter model running behind one local API on two NVIDIA DGX Stations, with every weight in GPU memory. That opens up work that’s hard to do on a hosted endpoint: running inference on sensitive or proprietary data, prototyping agents locally, and iterating on prompts without per-token costs.
Connect your own application using the vLLM serving documentation, then rerun AIPerf with your prompts to find the concurrency that fits your workload. A frontier-scale model is now ready to build on, right from your desk.

articles.title: Nvidia director sold nearly $1B in stock weeks before the Jensen Huang scandal
articles.body:
Nvidia director sold nearly $1B in stock weeks before the Jensen Huang scandal broke — and no trading plan was flagged
Nvidia's second-largest shareholder sold about $946 million in company stock in the months leading up to CEO Jensen Huang's resignation on Nov. 12.
Nvidia [NASDAQ: NVDA] Board Director Mark Stevens was one of the top AI sellers in Q3 2026, selling roughly 4.2 million shares, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. There were three separate batches of stock sales from Stevens, who joined the Nvidia board in 2008 following an earlier stint as a director from 1993 to 2006.
Must Read
- Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one
- Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP
- A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change
The first common stock sale took place from Aug. 31 to Sept. 2 at equity prices ranging from $220 to $226, generating $411 million in new cash. The second sale stretched from Sept. 3 to Sept. 4 at prices ranging between $227 to $234 per share, garnering about $236 million. The third sale occurred on Sept. 18 at roughly $220 per share, netting roughly $300 million.
Still holding plenty of Nvidia stock
Prearranged trading plans are used by executives to buy or sell shares of their firm on specific dates or target prices. It's a mechanism to wall off company employees from insider trading accusations as long as they stick to the automatic plan.
The SEC first instituted the practice in 2000 and modified it in 2022 to include a 90-day waiting period for starting trades. In some cases, the plans were abused by executives in instances like executing share sales just before an earnings report.
In Stevens's case, he didn't have such a trading plan, but that's not necessarily a red flag on its own. Insiders cashing out of their stock will do so for a variety of reasons that aren't always tied to a company's performance, such as quickly raising liquidity. In Nvidia's case, the move could pour water on the enthusiasm of retail investors to buy into an AI titan that has also attracted short sellers.
The first two stock sales in late August and early September followed a robust Q2 earnings report that caused Nvidia shares to jump about 10% in valuein the following week. Stevens still holds about 27.5 million shares in Nvidia, a colossal position.

articles.title: A gadget to make your dumb house smarter
articles.body:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 152, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, thank you for taking time away from Zelda to be here, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
A gadget to make your dumb house smarter
Plus, in this week’s Installer: a Space Race history, an Apple TV heist flick, a Wikipedia podcast, and much more.
This week, I’ve been reading about school apps and AI benches and sports gambling and Megaspeed, watching the surprisingly emotional Dane Cook documentary, learning way more than I ever expected about dial-up sounds, digging out my old Xbox One since it’s apparently my best shot at playing GTA VI, seeing what I can get done with Claude Duet, and trying a bunch of third-party iPhone keyboards in the hope of voice-typing my way through everything forever.
I also have for you a great new space history performance, new apps for writers and podcast listeners, a fun podcast about Wikipedia, and much more. Let’s dig in.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you watching / reading / playing / listening to / warming up on the stove this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- The Home Assistant Connect Aux-2. A very simple box that helps you add devices to your smart home (with particular emphasis on music gear), which also kind of acts as a universal controller for all the Bluetooth devices and dumb appliances in your house. Nothing you couldn’t build yourself, but much easier than doing so.
- We Chose to Go to the Moon. I was blown away by this live history of the Space Race, complemented by great music and beautiful visuals. Such a cool way to present a story like this, and kept me hooked the whole two hours. I would have watched a bunch more.
- TK. A new app from Medium with a bunch of really interesting ideas about how to share your ideas and work with other people without having to do it completely in public. Also just a nice web and mobile app for writing! I’m here for anything that makes people want to blog again.
- Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death. From what I’ve seen so far, this is a pretty unsparing look at the horrifying things men are doing to themselves in the name of becoming more attractive. Turns out the story goes back much further than Clavicular, and comes from some pretty bleak places.
- Tripod. A lovely new podcast app from Ben Rice McCarthy, who also makes a great camera app and a great social app and is just very good at apps. It has some clever organization features, but it’s also just really well designed, and that is a rare thing to find in a podcast app.
- 12 12 12. The consensus seems to be that this new Apple TV heist thriller might be too clever by half, but what I’ve seen so far is also just a lot of fun. And at this point? Apple’s track record is good enough that I’ll give almost any new title a few episodes.
- Click Through. I am wildly jealous of this podcast idea: Two hosts play The Wikipedia Game, trying to get from one thing to another as fast as possible, narrating and going on tangents the whole way. The first episode is very funny and a very good hang, and I… learned a lot about Greenwich Village?
- Google Tabletop. This is just an early prototype of an app, but I love the idea: a collaborative workspace like a Google Doc that can take the form of whatever tool or mini app you need. I immediately have 100 uses for it; I hope Google doesn’t immediately kill it.
- The Ring Drone Cam. A drone that can go inspect and see anything in your house: useful! Also terrifying dystopia hellscape! I am desperately curious to know everything about how this $250 gizmo works — though I can tell you confidently my wife will never allow it in our house.
A lot of you out there in the Installerverse have become iPhone Duo users over the last few weeks, and I’ve heard a lot about how you’re all using Apple’s new foldable phone. (I’d say the sentiment in my inbox is roughly 80 percent positive, 5 percent negative, 15 percent deeply confused about interface choices.) I’ve also gotten some questions about which Duo apps are great, and how best to set yours up.
Alas, I do not have a Duo. So I turned to The Verge’s Allison Johnson, who coauthored our review of the device and has used it as aggressively as anyone I know. I asked her to share how she’s wielding the Duo, and she sent over a truly unhinged color scheme and otherwise a bunch of very good ideas. Her’s her homescreen, plus some info on the apps she uses and why:
The phone: iPhone Duo.
The wallpaper: It’s one of those color gradient options you can pick in iOS. I was trying to go for a minimalist thing.
The apps: NYT Games, Kindle, Headspace, Spotify, Google Maps, Safari, Messages, Mail.
So I tried the whole aspirational “dress for the homescreen you want” thing for a few days, with just a few apps like Headspace and NYT Games, and it was a miserable failure. It just made me mad every time I had to search for Messages. I added a row of essential apps to the bottom of the screen and a big calendar widget, and things have been much better.
There’s a big widget / shortcut to TypeDraw, which is a fantastic app on the Duo that makes the whole phone behave like a physical notebook. It’s great with the Apple Pencil. I also realized I need weather close by, so I added a giant widget to the left panel of the homescreen.
I also have a shortcut for the built-in lo-fi playlists on iOS, which is handy if I need to pop in earbuds and play something instrumental so I can focus real quick. Highly recommended to anyone who hasn’t discovered these yet and also gets overstimulated! They’re already on your phone!
I did nuke the dock entirely in my minimalist experiment and I’m actually fine with it. Maybe I’ll never go back to the dock again.
I also asked Allison to share a few things she’s into right now. Here’s what she sent back:
- I don’t have a Switch 2 so I’m having extreme Zelda FOMO right now. I WISH I was playing Ocarina of Time but I’m just playing through every last bit of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on my PS5 to distract myself.
- I’m like 20 minutes away from finishing Widow’s Bay and that has been a really fun watch.
- I just finished reading the Planet Money book, which is like, The Economy For Dummies. It’s pretty entertaining and was very helpful for an economy dummy like me.
- I also got a book called Coffee, For Here by an award-winning barista and creator named Morgan Eckroth. They have lots of specialty drink recipes you can make with a home espresso setup. I made one over the weekend and I’m still thinking about how good it was. The photos are beautiful too.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week.
“Search, a browser developed by a small Parisian design studio of all things. I’d say they have created the classy European cousin of Arc, based on Webkit so it’s super light & responsive on Mac while also having the flexibility of Chrome extensions.” — Elliot
“Trying out Monarch to potentially break my years-long Quicken habit. So far I’m about 90% sure I’m switching.” — Bruce
“Dungeon Crawler Carl. I recently started listening to the audiobook. It has consumed my life. I listen to it on my drive to work, I take breaks at work to listen to it, I play it throughout my day, and eventually fall asleep listening to it. It’s almost 200 hours of content and Jeff Hays does an amazing job voicing all the characters. I’m currently on book seven of eight, and not looking forward to the withdrawals as we wait for book 9. Seriously, check it out.” — William
“Brenpoly on YouTube has open-sourced his “I built an Apple Vision Pro for $5” project. It’s a great watch even if you don’t dabble in 3D printing. It also shows how much potential there is for affordable VR with just the phones in our pockets and some very clever people and communities.” — Owen
“For anyone with an iPhone Duo. On the outer display, Safari keeps a column down the side for its buttons, and web pages stop short of it. I’m a Duo owner, and am now using a great Safari extension called Widen that runs pages underneath that column: ~25% more page, with text kept clear of the buttons.” — Marcus
“I took my kid to see Wildwood, the new Laika movie, this past weekend and left the theater with my jaw on the floor and dragging a few feet behind me. It is extraordinary. For me, put it up there with the all time Studio Ghibli greats. (I know, I know, but I’m serious.) In a way that no Marvel movie special effects have done, I sat at multiple times in the movie thinking, ‘I just can’t believe humans made this.’” — Stephen
“I am a browser snob, constantly flitting back and forth trying to find the one that combines speed with features with proper UX with privacy. I had begrudgingly settled on Safari for Apple and Chrome for everything else when I stumbled upon Brave Origin. It’s a little steep at a one-time purchase of $59, but it’s completely cross platform, syncs, and gets rid of all the Brave cruft. It’s just a good, minimal, fast Chromium-based browser.” — Kait
“Queen’s Domain, a wonderful King’s Field-like game, was released this past weekend and it conjures up all those familiar FromSoftware feelings of combat and exploration! Highly recommended, it’s quite the experience.” — Kyle
“I finished Jet Lag: The Game’s Japanorama, and it is the absolute best tourism video series for Japan without trying at all to be one. It is part scavenger hunt, part race across Japan, and shows off the wonderful scenery and the beautiful public transit of the country. I learnt that Japan loves making lists (OCD folks rejoice!) and has lists of Three Views, Three Great Gardens, 100 Best Sunsets, 100 Remarkable Waters and many more.” — Utkarsh
Signing off
I’m working on a story about the new era of hardware hacking, in which people are suddenly discovering they can vibe-code their way to a better TV, the e-reader of their dreams, and a million other things besides. In almost all my conversations, one thing keeps coming up: the M5Stack developer kits. This company will send you an ESP32-based device you can hack to bits, whether you’re looking for something with an E Ink display or something with a round touchscreen. I’m about to spend an alarming amount of money buying these things, and an equally alarming amount of time making Claude Code do weird stuff with them. I’m already stealing ideas from the fabulous M5Stack subreddit. If you get up to something fun while hardware hacking this weekend, tell me all about it.
See you next week!

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
articles.body:
It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.
Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.
Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.
“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.
Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.
Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.
“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”
Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.
For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.
“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”
It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.
If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.
Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.
While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.
Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.
Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.
“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.
Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

articles.title: Live-migration support in FreeBSD and bhyve coming
articles.body:
This project presents a first working state for live migration of bhyve guests on FreeBSD 15.1. A running amd64 guest can move between two hosts over TCP while continuing to run; it is paused only for the final stop-and-copy phase. The work builds on bhyve's experimental snapshot support and adds dirty-page tracking in the vmm kernel module together with a migration protocol in bhyve and bhyvectl.
I previously discussed the state of bhyve live migration, its historical development, existing limitations, and why it matters for the future of FreeBSD virtualization in my article bhyve on FreeBSD and VM Live Migration – Quo vadis?.
The goal is deliberately practical: make it possible to test, discuss, and improve a real implementation rather than discuss live migration only in the abstract. The current code and test tooling are being published as a WIP RFC so that the next steps can be shaped in the open. A more detailed demonstration of a VM being live migrated can be watched on my YouTube channel.
Why this matters
Live migration is an important building block for enterprise virtualisation. It enables host maintenance, hardware replacement, load balancing, and failure-domain management with far less disruption to workloads. It is also central to the Sylve project, which aims to offer a Proxmox-like virtualisation solution for FreeBSD. Migration is not an optional convenience in that kind of platform; it is one of the capabilities that makes clustered operations practical.
It is equally important for BoxyBSD, where I offer free BSD-based VPS instances to individuals. Without a credible migration path, routine host work can require a guest outage. That makes live migration a current show stopper for the project, and is why this work is being pushed toward a testable, reviewable state.
How the current implementation works
The source starts with a pre-copy phase. It sends populated guest memory, then repeatedly obtains a bitmap of pages changed since the previous scan and sends only those pages. Once the remaining dirty set fits the configured downtime target, stops shrinking, or reaches the configured round limit, bhyve pauses the guest and its devices. It then sends the final dirty pages and the existing snapshot state for the vCPUs, kernel state, and emulated devices.
The destination validates the basic VM geometry, receives memory and state, restores it, and reports that it is ready. Only then does the source send GO, the commit point. Before GO, a failed migration can resume the source guest. The destination does not start the guest if it does not receive that commit message. A warm, stop-and-copy mode is available too, which is useful both as a fallback and as a comparison baseline.
What is implemented today
- Pre-copy and warm migration: live pre-copy is configurable with downtime and maximum-round controls; explicit stop-and-copy migration is also supported.
- Multi-vCPU protocol support: the migration handshake carries the guest vCPU count, the destination refuses a count mismatch, and all guest vCPUs are paused and resumed as part of migration. The published test bed has primarily exercised a one-vCPU guest, so multi-vCPU stress and race testing remain required before making broader claims.
- Memory consistency checks: dirty-page tracking covers guest and mapped emulation writes through page dirty state, while vmm write holds are recorded separately. The test workload rewrites and verifies guest memory and reports any missing or stale page as a mismatch. Repeated ping-pong migrations have been used to check that the workload continues without errors.
- Disk-write validation: a guest-side workload repeatedly writes and fsyncs files, verifies checksums, and is checked again after a cold reboot. This is intended to exercise the device pause, drain, and restore path.
- Failure handling: destination refusal, an unreachable target, and a target disappearing during both pre-copy and stop-and-copy have been tested. Before commit, the source is intended to resume the paused guest after failure.
- Basic destination checks: protocol version, page size, memory layout, and vCPU count are checked before data transfer. The migration socket is opened by bhyvectl and passed into bhyve so that bhyve can remain inside its Capsicum sandbox.
- Supported scope: this is amd64-only and depends on the experimental BHYVE_SNAPSHOT support. It relies on snapshot-capable emulated devices; PCI passthrough is not migratablem, yet.
Observed results
In the current two-host test environment, repeated live migrations, memory-rewrite workloads, and fsync-heavy disk workloads have completed successfully. For a slowly dirtying 512 MiB guest, observed downtime has been roughly 138–171 ms. A rapidly dirtying guest may not converge during pre-copy, but still falls back to a correct stop-and-copy completion with a longer pause. These are encouraging engineering results, not a production support promise or a complete correctness proof.
Blockers before upstreaming can be evaluated further
The following are neutral engineering requirements, not criticism of the value of the prototype. They need to be addressed first before further upstreaming into FreeBSD can be evaluated responsibly.
- Prove and harden dirty-log correctness. The kernel-side dirty-page algorithm must be demonstrated not to lose a write while dirty bits are examined and cleared. It needs focused concurrency, paging, emulation-write, and multi-vCPU stress coverage, plus a reviewable locking and memory-ordering argument.
- Define a complete compatibility contract. Matching memory size and vCPU count is not enough. A destination should verify guest identity, CPU capabilities, bhyve/vmm and snapshot format compatibility, device topology and capabilities, and shared-storage identity before accepting a migration.
- Harden the transport and protocol. The current TCP transport has no authentication or encryption and uses a first-version native protocol. A stable protocol needs explicit wire formats, bounded message handling, timeouts, version negotiation, authentication or a supported external secure transport model, and clear operational guidance.
- Clarify the commit and device-side-effect boundary. The source/destination handoff must be reviewed so that device restoration cannot cause externally visible work before the source has committed, and so that the unavoidable uncertain outcome after a lost post-commit acknowledgement is operationally recoverable.
- Specify storage and network handoff. Shared storage must have defined coherency, durability, and fencing assumptions. Network migration also needs a clear answer for tap/bridge handling, MAC/IP movement, and traffic convergence.
- Build an in-tree test strategy. The current scripts and test-bed workloads are useful, but upstream review will need automated regression coverage and a documented support matrix across CPU counts, memory sizes, supported devices, host CPUs, and failure cases.
- Separate the work into reviewable patches. Dirty-page tracking, snapshot API refactoring, protocol/receiver work, CLI changes, and tests should be independently reviewable. This will make design feedback more actionable and reduce the risk of merging coupled changes.
Next steps
We have already had deeper discussions about these questions in the Sylve Discord. Publishing this current state is intended to make those discussions more concrete, bring in wider FreeBSD and bhyve feedback, and turn the prototype into a clear roadmap. The immediate focus is correctness, compatibility validation, transport safety, and repeatable tests—not adding performance features first. Currently, some peopel already have access to it and it's planned ot publish this at least as a proposal on my git and GitHub at:
- git.gyptazy.com/gyptazy/freebsd-bhyve-live-migration
- github.com/gyptazy/freebsd-bhyve-live-migration
Compression, zero-page elision, broader device coverage, richer orchestration, and performance tuning can follow once the foundation is sound. If you operate bhyve, work on FreeBSD virtualisation, or are interested in Sylve or BoxyBSD, testing the RFC and contributing design feedback would be especially valuable.
Status: WIP RFC for a first working bhyve live-migration implementation on FreeBSD 15.1.

articles.title: 6-11X speedup running Qwen3.6 on my RTX 4090, full repo.
articles.body:
Lightreason is a local inference lab and interactive Studio for running Qwen faster on one RTX 4090. The experiments use the original BF16 weights for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (3.09B parameters) and the text model of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (34.66B parameters).
- 3B · 63.0 → 139.6 tok/s across six prompts. LR CUDA graphs and compact KV matched all 30 Hugging Face timing runs. It also matched complete Python, JavaScript, and SQL responses in 9/9 new pairs. The separate PARD2 runner reached 58.3 → 525.2 tok/s on a complete matching weather response and 63.6 → 724.4 tok/s on the best matching 128-token Fibonacci slice. Performance · Coding benchmarks
- 35B · 7.93 → 51.08 tok/s on the capped Python prompt. The 6.44× comparison uses the same input across sessions. Output first differs from Scheduled at token 116. The packed configuration matched all 20 pairs against its closer fixed eight-position control. Performance · Coding results and output checks
The smaller model fits on the GPU, where reusing prepared GPU work and checking several tokens together saves time. The larger model’s text weights occupy 64.56 GiB. The 35B runner keeps most expert weights in system RAM and moves the ones Qwen actually uses. When a draft predicts several tokens, Qwen checks them together and can reuse weights across those checks. The original BF16 Qwen target makes every final token decision.
LR labels configurations we built and measured. They use existing techniques and projects, including NVIDIA CUDA Graphs, AMD PARD2, Inco AI DFlash2, and FlashML’s FreeToken. The experiment history credits those projects, details Lightreason’s changes, and records which experiments slowed down or changed the output.
Live Studio is a simple, interactive way to test speed. Build and preview a web page, then run the same prompt through Standard and Lightreason Exact to watch each response stream and compare its timings.
Run 3B Studio · Coding benchmarks · Experiment history · Reproduce 35B · Port to other hardware
The GitHub checkout contains source, pinned download manifests, and benchmark evidence. It ships zero checkpoint or adapter weights. Download the models you need on the GPU machine.
If you only want 3B Studio, a sparse clone skips the 35B sources and benchmark archives.
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/me-farza/lightreason.git
git -C lightreason sparse-checkout set demo_chat results3b
The 3B PARD2 peak numbers are archived research measurements. The public PARD2 weights require the matching lab adapter to reproduce those numbers. The target-only 3B results use the public Qwen download alone.
The public 3B Studio quickstart uses Linux with an RTX 4090 and a driver compatible with CUDA 12.8. Standard and Lightreason Exact use only the Qwen target. Your browser can run on a different machine. The 35B runners use a separate benchmark setup with a larger system RAM requirement. With the sparse checkout, start at cd lightreason below. 35B setup
Install Python 3.12, its venv package and headers, and a C compiler for Triton. On Ubuntu 24.04, install build-essential python3.12-venv python3.12-dev. Run nvidia-smi on the GPU machine to confirm the driver sees the card. The download is about 6.2 GB and the downloader requires another 2 GiB of free space. Budget separately for Python packages and compilation caches.
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/me-farza/lightreason.git
cd lightreason
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install 'torch==2.9.1' --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -c 'import torch; name = torch.cuda.get_device_name(); print(name); assert "4090" in name and torch.version.hip is None and torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported()'
python download_3b.py --destination model-3b
python -m demo_chat.server --model-path model-3b
The setup pins PyTorch 2.9.1 with CUDA 12.8 and Transformers 4.57.1. download_3b.py checks the official objects against the pinned download plan. Read the Qwen license before downloading or using the model. Qwen license · Original v0.1.0 source
Leave the server running and open http://127.0.0.1:8765/. For a remote GPU, first run this tunnel in a separate terminal on your browser machine.
ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:8765:127.0.0.1:8765 YOUR_GPU_HOST
- Wait for Qwen to load. You can check for "ready": true with curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/status.
- Open Compare runners, select Qwen · Lightreason Exact, choose a sample prompt, and click Run comparison. Studio runs Standard first and then Exact on the same GPU and compares the full token sequences.
- Repeat the same prompt to see warm performance. Exact prepares graphs automatically, and Studio reports preparation separately from generation. Use Save results to export the timings and match result. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.
For a headless smoke test, run the same prompt and token cap through each CLI engine. The JSON records preparation, generation, token IDs, and stop reason. Use Studio or the repeated benchmark harness for speed measurements.
python run_model_3b.py --model-path model-3b --engine original --tokens 128 --json --prompt 'Explain why the sky is blue.'
python run_model_3b.py --model-path model-3b --engine bucketed --tokens 128 --json --prompt 'Explain why the sky is blue.'
Lightreason Exact records and replays GPU work, keeps a compact attention cache, combines BF16 projections, and screens vocabulary candidates before scoring survivors with the original output weights. The draft-assisted 3B runner verifies candidate trees and coordinates acceptance on the GPU. On 36 held-out comparisons it was 1.062× faster with the same outputs as the preceding draft-assisted runner. It matched Hugging Face on 12/36. Implementation and reproduction
For 35B, FreeToken and DFlash2 provide the hybrid CPU/GPU executor and parallel draft. Lightreason adds selected-row prefill, AVX2 reuse across repeated expert routes, native CUDA unpack, packed host banks on 34 layers, and a lossless GPU replica tier. It reconstructs the original BF16 bits before the expert math. Runtime, profiles, and reproduction
For other hardware, measure the unmodified model on your device first. Use the porting guide to identify whether GPU work, memory, or transfers limit the full request. From the cloned repository, ask Codex to use $lightreason-hardware. With another coding agent, point it at the hardware skill.
Open Build preview to generate single-file HTML and render it in the sandboxed preview. Studio reports generation and browser rendering separately.
New app generates a page. Edit current app supplies its HTML and asks Qwen for the full update. Patch edit (experimental) asks Qwen for one small JSON search-and-replace, checks it against the current HTML, and renders the reconstructed document after successful completion. Use the full edit path for larger changes or to retry a rejected patch. A successful patch currently reloads the sandboxed preview, which restarts page state.
The two patch formats, their local HTTP benchmarks, and known failures are described in the benchmark notes.
Standard and Exact run with the target checkpoint alone. The optional Turbo runner and the GPU coordination benchmark additionally require the pinned AMD PARD2 draft directory and the matching trained LoRA/projector checkpoint supplied locally. See the optional setup and reproduction commands. That adapter is separate from this source release.
Run the CPU-side Studio contract tests from the repository root:
python -m unittest discover -s demo_chat -p 'test_*.py'
node demo_chat/test_preview.js
Original Lightreason source and documentation use 0BSD. FreeToken patches and the Qwen checkpoints have separate upstream terms. Lightreason license · Third-party terms and credits · Lightreason logo

articles.title: Big tech is here to let us down
articles.body:
When I woke up this morning I thought about writing about the ongoing drama surrounding Nvidia and its morally and ethically corrupt leader. But, then I quickly saw the news about Microsoft Outlook going down, and with it Teams and Copilot.
I soon saw many employees celebrating what effectively became a "snow day for adults" as they literally couldn't do their jobs. Then I started seeing various businesses, ranging from small to medium, saying that their normal support services are unsurprisingly not working and instead to contact them via social media. Except, it's not just businesses that are impacted by Microsoft's incompetence. Even if this is some legitimate accident (and not a more likely instance of someone vibecoding their way via Copilot), when a company like Microsoft fires tens of thousands of employees, including many engineers, then these problems are not only more likely, but also more difficult to quickly fix. The fact that this has actually been an issue across two separate days is pathetic for a company like Microsoft.
As beyond businesses impacted, all sorts of other entities have been impacted. Various forms of educational institutions from schools to universities as well as the courts! I wouldn't be surprised if healthcare has been impacted as well.
Now, are Microsoft going to offer any compensation for either lost business or additional accrued costs? I highly doubt it, even though it is literally their fault and they do still have the cash reserves, despite increasingly wasting it on loss-making AI adventures.
This is a reminder of how indebted the Global North has become to Microsoft and its enshittified services. If most (but thankfully not all) businesses and institutions are deep into Microsoft systems, then when Microsoft inevitably messes up again, large swathes of organisations will not be able to function properly. Yes, it might be good for the individual worker in a generic office role, but for keyworker type organisations this can have really damaging implications. Many European state institutions have already started the move away from Microsoft to open source alternatives. Largely to not be at the mercy of an inconsistent United States of America, but also for times like this. As when Microsoft services go down, you cannot fix it! You have to wait for Microsoft to find a competent employee who wasn't let go to try and fix what was broken by some inept leftover who was deluded enough to think that Copilot can do everything.
I still want to talk about the issues of the impact of other US company Nvidia and the implications it has around the world. But that can wait for another day. Plus, who knows if another affairs comes out (we're currently at three).

articles.title: Models can now transmit viruses in weight-space
articles.body:
Submitted 14 Nov 2026
Weight Space Misfolding
Abstract
Weight space editing changes a neural network’s knowledge, behaviour and alignment through direct modification of its weights. Model-mediated weight space manipulation, also known as weight space programming or intra-weight injection, has emerged as a capability of advanced frontier models. While it offers benefits for gradient-free adaptation, it also creates an opportunity for one model to induce unauthorised behaviour in another. We call this weight space misfolding, by analogy with protein misfolding in prion disease, and consider both direct interference and hypothetical onward propagation. The asymmetry between an attacker seeking a harmful intervention, who merely needs to generate the payload attack once, and a defender who needs to find that needle in the haystack of weights, creates an impossible choice for the latter: they can either prohibit weight editing altogether, forfeiting its benefits, or be bound to cover the burden and cost. We develop a threat model and a non-exhaustive taxonomy covering factual substitution, capability denial and selective omission, including offensive uses of selective unlearning, then illustrate it on the basis of three selected case studies using the IWIBench interface. We find that while targeted disruption is possible, the limitations in reliability and functional preservation are significant. While the cases explored in this paper do not demonstrate self-propagation or actual offensive capabilities, it is abundantly clear that the building blocks are present and identifiable in frontier models. While these cases by no means directly establish self-propagation, they show why imperfect editing capabilities can still pose a security risk. We examine defensive approaches, including control of the path from authorised editing to deployment, acceptance and recovery requirements and the implications for physical AI.
From the authors
View full on X
The dark side of weight space programming: viruses that spread in model weights.
Meet weight space misfolding, a novel kind of malware wherein models infect other models - potentially allowing frontier models to reach into air gapped environments.
At present, no public model exists that can reliably perform the steps needed to effectuate weight space misfolding. We need to be clear about this. But in just five months, the underlying capability doubled (from 5.6-Sol to 6.1-Sol). This is the time to prepare.
Show full threadShow less
Huge props to @tfoldi, @Pranavdoma0323 and that other guy who needs a twitter account for the work leading up to this, as well as to our partners.

articles.title: Palmfrets, Minnesota guitarist's invention, strikes a new chord
articles.body:
FERGUS FALLS — The back room of Stella’s restaurant in Fergus Falls filled with people on Oct. 28, all there to see musician Ben Ranson play.
Ranson, who grew up in Sebeka, Minnesota, and currently lives in Sandstone, is a regular performer at venues across the region, including in Fergus Falls. But Oct. 28 was no ordinary gig. That night, Ranson revealed something he’d been working on for years.
ADVERTISEMENT
It wasn’t a new song or a clever guitar lick, it was an invention called “palmfrets” — something Ranson believes could change the way guitarists use their instrument. It allows players to play new bass lines or melodies using their palm, a special set of frets called palmfrets and a technique called palmfretting.
The invention
The idea for palmfrets came to Ranson over five years ago.
Ranson had already been doing musical experiments — even constructing organ-like foot pedals and learning the seven string guitar — all in a quest to get more notes out of the guitar, specifically more bass notes.
He said the reason behind the invention, initially, was entirely artistic. He wasn’t thinking much about developing a commercial product.
“That was not on my mind at all,” Ranson said. “And it wasn’t really until I made one that really worked that it sort of dawned on me like, oh, this is something that people are really going to want.”
Ranson made an early-stage version of the invention in his garage, and said that, at first, he didn't recognize the importance of what he had created. He set it aside and left it in a corner for awhile — years, even.
Eventually, he returned to his forgotten creation. It was then that he began to hear the music.
ADVERTISEMENT
He drafted his ideas and designs on paper, and enlisted the help of engineers. Together, they created new prototypes made from 3D printed plastic and laser-cut metal parts.
It was during that time when Ranson said something shifted.
“It hit me, like, I’ve really done it.”
Ranson knew the plastic and metal version was not practical, and only lasted a matter of weeks. But it worked, and from there, Ranson said the engineering became more serious.
Serious enough that Ranson applied for a patent, which he received on Oct. 6, 2026.
Ranson had an inkling that this was something special, and recalled the first time he started playing the guitar with a solid prototype.
“I was like, ‘I’m doing things that Chet Atkins never did,’” he joked. “I just had this sort of realization, like, other people are going to want to do this.”
ADVERTISEMENT
Fast forward to Oct. 28 in Fergus Falls, and Ranson’s invention is now in the hands of other guitar players.
How it works
Using the pisiform bone — a small, pea-shaped bone in the wrist, near the bottom of the palm — players depress a string on the palmfret, an extra fret or set of frets near the wrist of the picking hand. The player can then use the thumb of their picking hand to pluck the string fretted by the pisiform bone.
This frees up the fretting hand — the hand which frets strings on the neck of the guitar — meaning the player can move up and down the fret board more freely, and fret other strings because the pisiform bone is doing some of the hard work.
“So if you want to, you can move (the fretting hand) anywhere you want, play any other notes that you want to play,” said Ranson.
Essentially, guitarists could play a bass line with their pisiform bone and play other melodies or chords that would have otherwise been, literally, out of reach.
Learning curve
Ranson had some rules when designing palmfrets.
“One of the basic principles in inventing it has been: if it interferes with the normal way that you would play the guitar, it’s no good,” he said.
ADVERTISEMENT
“So the basic principle is you have to keep all of the function of the guitar as people know it,” he explained. “It has to add, but it can’t take away. That’s the basic principle.”
Still, adding another element to the guitar introduces a learning curve, even for players as skilled as Ranson.
He gave proof of the learning curve by showing a callus on his pisofone bone — a callus reminiscent of the ones beginning guitarists get on their fingers when first learning to play — and compared his skill-level with the palmfrets to being a teenager playing in their first band and only knowing six songs.
“That is the stage I am at now, frankly.”
During the reveal, other guitar players tested out the palmfrets, taking turns passing around acoustic guitars, electric, and even the bass.
Darren Quam, a musician from Battle Lake, who was in attendance on Oct. 28, tried his hand — or palm — at the new invention.
“At first, you know, it took me a second to kind of understand how you could use it,” Quam said. “But then — especially when Ben had us come up and try it — then, you know, trying it with my own hands, I was like, okay, I see how this could be very useful in certain situations.”
ADVERTISEMENT
Quam also commented on the learning curve.
“It’s not a whole new instrument, but it’s a whole new way of playing.”
Despite the new way of playing, during the reveal show, Quam seemed to catch on quickly, with Ranson joking “we’re going to have to take this away from you.”
From a practical standpoint as a gigging musician, Quam thought the invention would be useful for solo players.
“I think it really is probably the most useful in like a solo situation where you’re playing and you can accompany yourself, especially with those lower notes where you can fret with your palm hand and change the root note or the chords, and still be able to have the freedom to play on the higher strings as if there was someone else accompanying you, you know, like a bass player.
“So it’s kind of like you’ve got a bass player on your palm all of a sudden.”
And speaking of bass players, Ranson believes the bass guitar, as it now is, could become “obsolete.”
ADVERTISEMENT
“But for a great reason, as far as bassists are concerned,” he said.
With the palmfrets, a bass player could play a bass line beneath a bass line, or play chords while playing a bass line. Meaning a bass player could accompany themselves, or add chords when playing with a group.
“As a guitarist, you might want to play some jazz song, or whatever song you want — it’s got a clear melody, but you just need to have chords underneath it so that people can understand what that melody is.”
With palmfrets, the bass player can play the chord and the bass line, rooting the listener, while allowing the lead guitarist to focus on the melody.
Ranson explained that he expects the invention to make the bass into a very powerful instrument, “kind of like a piano.”
The future
For Ranson, thinking about how the invention will be used in the future is all speculation.
“But I think it’s going to be really interesting. I mean, I can’t wait,” said Ranson.
The true potential of the invention, according to Ranson, might not be revealed for many years.
“Let’s say 15 years from now, there’s going to be some kid who got one of these as a teenager. Then you’ll know what it can do.”

articles.title: How Not to Build a Music Player
articles.body:
The Twelve-Day War made me realize online music players aren’t a viable option for those who live under an oppressive regime that disconnects the internet across the country as a way to silence public opinion.
So, as soon as the connection came back, I started archiving tracks and looking for offline alternatives and discovered Strawberry. It’s a feature-rich music player and kept me happy for quite a while, but I have this habit of looking at song lyrics and singing along! Strawberry fetches lyrics from the internet when it recognizes a song, but sometimes the lyrics weren’t line-synced and worse, it displayed the timestamps next to the lyrics which I found pretty annoying to look at. I wasn’t aware of other music players such as foobar2000 which my friend just pointed me to while writing this post.
I decided to write my own music player and call it AMP with a few goals in mind: minimal feature-set, no C++ dependencies, proper system integration to make it feel like a native app, and of course, write it in Zig (including the shaders!). I also wanted to roll my own UI because of the fun memories of working on V’s UI during my first days of being introduced into system programming. But before I could make any meaningful progress, a new wave of protests started. Following the tragedy of January 8 and 9, another internet blackout began, lasting more than four months.
During the blackout, there were these anonymous people on Telegram selling internet access through personal White SIMs, whitelisted servers, Starlink dishes, etc. A black market had formed for the freaking internet! You’d get charged $5 or more for just 1GB of traffic. The prices dropped slightly after a while, but it was still hella expensive. The regime surely made a lot of money out of it. I ended up spending hundreds of dollars on these services and other methods just to stay in touch with my friends and keep my hobbies alive. Killing time was becoming a problem. Especially for someone like me who built their entire social life online.
I carefully used this slow connection to download repositories, documention, etc. to continue working on my music player. It really brought me immense joy during this hard time.
Once the connection was mostly restored to the pre-blackout days (UDP traffic is still blocked, though, which naturally also affects QUIC), my attention was shifted towards LLMs. It had become very hard for me to ignore the hype and progress around frontier LLMs. As I really never thought about using them seriously for coding. They are still everywhere in the news, and I was just reminded that I owned a Claude Max 20x subscription gift from my boss back in 2025. Eating dust and maybe soon expiring. So I decided to give it a try and experiment on my music player. It was a very addictive experience. I literally couldn’t hit the plan limits no matter how hard I tried, so after a few non-stop days of prompting, a good chunk of AMP was vibecoded..
At the time, I thought this was an okay approach for a hobby project and I could just un-slopify it later. Little did I know I’m mentally incapable of reviewing tens of thousands lines of code. Shortly after, Anthropic figured that I live in Iran and instantly banned my account. Then Codeberg announced its no-AI policy, which gave me two choices. Either get rid of all that slop or move the repository elsewhere. Going with the former option, I started reading every single line of code, rewriting them. I was surprised by my own ignorance and how much LLMs like to complicate stuff. (I wish I could show an example, but my memory is extremely fragile and I’ve got no pre-rewrite history of the repo to check).
Four months later, nearly half the codebase is gone, and somehow it’s more robust with the same set of features (and more). I regret relying on LLMs in the first place, but hey, lesson learned. That said I think it’s still possible to create a healthy relationship with LLMs as long as you look at them as a fancy IDE feature. A lot of times they are just running long sed or regex commands that are a no-brainer act for humans when done by hand but still consumes a good time. For now and hopefully forever I think I’ll be going the old school way. Never rush your hobbies!
Btw this is how AMP looks like right now!
Worth mentioning that the blur shader is written in Zig based on this excellent blog post!.
Roadmap to v1.0:
- Music server
- Android and Windows support
- Packaging for major Linux distros
- Any suggestions?
