I also wanted to roll my own UI because of the fun memories of working on V’s UI during my first days of being introduced into system programming. But before I could make any meaningful progress, a new wave of protests started. Following the tragedy of January 8 and 9, another internet blackout began, lasting more than four months.
During the blackout, there were these anonymous people on Telegram selling internet access through personal White SIMs, whitelisted servers, Starlink dishes, etc. A black market had formed for the freaking internet! You’d get charged $5 or more for just 1GB of traffic. The prices dropped slightly after a while, but it was still hella expensive. The regime surely made a lot of money out of it. I ended up spending hundreds of dollars on these services and other methods just to stay in touch with my friends and keep my hobbies alive. Killing time was becoming a problem. Especially for someone like me who built their entire social life online.
I carefully used this slow connection to download repositories, documention, etc. to continue working on my music player. It really brought me immense joy during this hard time.
Once the connection was mostly restored to the pre-blackout days (UDP traffic is still blocked, though, which naturally also affects QUIC), my attention was shifted towards LLMs. It had become very hard for me to ignore the hype and progress around frontier LLMs. As I really never thought about using them seriously for coding. They are still everywhere in the news, and I was just reminded that I owned a Claude Max 20x subscription gift from my boss back in 2025. Eating dust and maybe soon expiring. So I decided to give it a try and experiment on my music player. It was a very addictive experience. I literally couldn’t hit the plan limits no matter how hard I tried, so after a few non-stop days of prompting, a good chunk of AMP was vibecoded..
At the time, I thought this was an okay approach for a hobby project and I could just un-slopify it later. Little did I know I’m mentally incapable of reviewing tens of thousands lines of code. Shortly after, Anthropic figured that I live in Iran and instantly banned my account. Then Codeberg announced its no-AI policy, which gave me two choices. Either get rid of all that slop or move the repository elsewhere. Going with the former option, I started reading every single line of code, rewriting them. I was surprised by my own ignorance and how much LLMs like to complicate stuff. (I wish I could show an example, but my memory is extremely fragile and I’ve got no pre-rewrite history of the repo to check).
Four months later, nearly half the codebase is gone, and somehow it’s more robust with the same set of features (and more). I regret relying on LLMs in the first place, but hey, lesson learned. That said I think it’s still possible to create a healthy relationship with LLMs as long as you look at them as a fancy IDE feature. A lot of times they are just running long sed or regex commands that are a no-brainer act for humans when done by hand but still consumes a good time. For now and hopefully forever I think I’ll be going the old school way. Never rush your hobbies!
Btw this is how AMP looks like right now!
Worth mentioning that the blur shader is written in Zig based on this excellent blog post!.
Roadmap to v1.0:
- Music server
- Android and Windows support
- Packaging for major Linux distros
- Any suggestions?

articles.title: ‘The Sacred Ordinary’ Shines a Light on Heritage in Birmingham’s Civil Rights District
articles.body:
‘The Sacred Ordinary’ Shines a Light on Heritage in Birmingham’s Civil Rights District
In the second stanza of “How to Be a Poet,” Wendell Berry wrote: “There are no unsacred places; / there are only sacred places / and desecrated places.” When it comes to preserving important historical locations, such as monuments, parks, and buildings, a new interactive public art installation asks, “what happens when preservation itself is endangered?”
The Sacred Ordinary is an initiative organized by 1504, a production studio based in Birmingham that emphasizes in-depth storytelling to connect people with meaningful, human-focused services and experiences. The participatory artwork is presented in collaboration with the National Parks Conservation Association, which aims to protect U.S. national parks for future generations.
In early 2025, President Trump issued an executive order that mandated the removal of some National Park Service signage relating to slavery, the LGBTQ+ community, climate change, and more, a move that erases histories inextricable from the nation’s identity. (The current administration has also blocked millions in funding for numerous parks and disrupted services.)
In Birmingham, the Civil Rights District is formally designated a national monument, comprising neighborhoods that Black people historically called home and where Jim Crow laws authorized segregation until the 1960s. The Civil Rights Movement reached a nexus here when activists Fred Shuttlesworth, Martin Luther King, Jr., and Ralph Abernathy, among many others, organized nonviolent marches in 1963, known today as the Birmingham Campaign. Police turned their dogs on demonstrators and used fire hoses on children. A bombing at a Baptist church killed four young Black girls.
The Sacred Ordinary venerates access to things most of us take for granted: the ability to shop at any store, attend the nearest school, walk around any neighborhood, and sit at the front of the bus. The exhibition is installed around-the-clock, but by day, elements of the installation comprise vintage yet mundane objects that one typically walks by without giving a second thought.
A huge midcentury television rests on an open lawn, and a red newspaper vending box for The Birmingham News, which ceased its print publication in 2012, advertises 25 cents per copy. Additional sites include a characteristically blue U.S. Postal Service mailbox and a walk-in telephone booth. Sheets of paper with tear-off tabs posted around town invite participants to learn more by texting a phone number. If you text “HERE” to the number, you’ll be directed to a starting point and an otherwise nondescript yellow fire hydrant.
In scavenger-hunt style, visitors are prompted to enter the year stamped on the unit, and if it’s between 5 and 8 p.m., the sequence of texted prompts doubles as a multimedia self-guided tour of Birmingham’s Civil Rights District like you’ve never seen it: the television screen, mailbox, phone booth, and more begin to glow once the sun has set.
“Birmingham, Alabama, is known around the world for such places—sites of civil rights history that many regard as sacred and that connect us to something larger than ourselves. But today, that memory is endangered,” 1504 says in a statement. “Aging infrastructure, the passing of a generation of foot soldiers, and federal efforts to erase chapters of American history raise an urgent question: if institutions alone cannot sustain history, what role can the public play in caring for sacred sites?”
Rather than center primarily on signage, The Sacred Ordinary focuses on objects associated with civic life in the mid-20th century, evoking collective memories and providing touchpoints for younger generations for whom boxy televisions, printed newspapers, and telephone booths feel distant from today’s experiences. Emblematic of the way news and information spread before the internet and smartphones, the objects confront visitors with not only the realities of how people organized and communicated during that time but also how those memories are preserved today. Even without didactics, objects and places carry meaning that no one can simply delete.
The tour opens with a narration by actor André Holland, who played a fundamental role in preserving a historic theater in nearby Bessemer, Alabama, and 1504 has dedicated the installation to Birmingham-based artist Joe Minter. The Sacred Ordinary continues nightly through December 13, with accompanying guided walks and other programs scheduled in the meantime. Learn more on the project’s website, and explore the studio’s work on Instagram. You might also be interested in “The Praise House,” directed by 1504’s Tyler Jones.

articles.title: Nvidia allegedly engineered scarcity by funding AI startups to buy its GPUs
articles.body:
Friday, November 13th 2026
NVIDIA Allegedly Engineered Scarcity By Funding AI Startups To Buy Its GPUs
Following the departure of now-former NVIDIA CEO, Jensen Huang, a new report by The Wall Street Journal (via Wccftech) has emerged alleging that NVIDIA artificially inflated the ongoing GPU and memory shortage by investing in AI startups that would go on to buy NVIDIA GPUs and build data centers. The reason behind this was to maintain the perception of ongoing high demand and to move an oversupply of semiconductors from TSMC. 
The WSJ report cites an August meeting between Huang and his senior finance team, including NVIDIA's CFO and acting CEO, Colette Kress, during which Kress pushed for a reduction in circular financing agreements, in response to which Huang allegedly lay into Kress, calling her a "deer in the headlights," after she had pushed to scale back NVIDIA's $250 billion deal with OpenAI. Jensen's push for further investment into small-scale cloud providers was seemingly in response to the changing tide that saw AI hyperscalers move away from off-the-shelf components in favor of custom solutions.The situation described in the report saw NVIDIA on the hook for an "avalanche" of GPUs from TSMC, for which it would have no immediate buyers. Part of the issue highlighted by Kress was also that these small-scale cloud providers NVIDIA was investing in could not afford to buy NVIDIA GPUs, meaning they, too, could be a financial dead end.
Sources:
				The Wall Street Journal, 				via Wccftech

articles.title: Amtrak booking system experiencing major issues amid nationwide FAA ground stop
articles.body:
Amtrak booking system returns to normal after outage during nationwide FAA ground stop
WASHINGTON - Amtrak said its booking system is returning to normal after a network outage that coincided with a nationwide FAA ground stop.
Users report outage
What we know:
Users on social media started sharing frustrations over ticket reservations Friday afternoon, with travelers showing error messages on Amtrak's website and app.
Hundreds of users reported issues on DownDetector, beginning shortly before 5 p.m. Friday, with another surge just before 6 p.m.
Issues caused by increased demand
What they're saying:
In response to a request for comment, Amtrak's Communications Director W. Kyle Anderson said that "Amtrak service is operating normally, and we are seeing increased demand for travel across our network."
Responding to a frustrated customer Friday, Amtrak officials said in a post on X that the booking issues were related to a system-wide update, but did not elaborate.
Around 9 p.m. officials said the booking systems were returning to normal.
The company said some customers may still experience issues while processing payments, booking trips or modifying existing reservations. Amtrak’s call centers experienced higher-than-normal call volumes, resulting in longer wait times for some.
FOX 5 DC attempted to call the support number during the outage, around 8 p.m., but an automated message said officials were unable to take calls due to "unusually high call volume."
Travelers scrambling during ground stop
The backstory:
The outage came as thousands of travelers across the country scrambled for new plans, after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop — the first since January 2023 and just the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
The FAA has said that the ground stop was ordered due to a "temporary telecommunications outage." It has since been lifted.
The Source: Information in this story is from social media posts commenting on the ticket booking outage, error messages on Amtrak's website and app, phone calls to Amtrak's support and media relations lines and previous FOX reporting on the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop.

articles.title: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
articles.body:
Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
By Sequoia Carrillo
Friday, November 13, 2026 • 5:00 AM EST
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework.
An announcement this month makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem.
Many parents do not.
"Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry."
Related Story: NPR
When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding limits on technology in the classroom.
But even as districts including Los Angeles Unified, Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.
In a post on X, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy.
A baffling move
Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.
She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google fended off in D.C.
Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search.
"The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court."
When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its original announcement, where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases.
NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether.
The "AI or nothing" approach
In any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs.
Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an "unacceptable risk" rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information.
The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina sued the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook.
Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois.
Related Story: NPR
"It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said.
Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI.
He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging.
"Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school."
The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well.
Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen
Google is a financial supporter of NPR.

articles.title: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
articles.body:
Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
By Sequoia Carrillo
Friday, November 13, 2026 • 5:00 AM EST
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework.
An announcement this month makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem.
Many parents do not.
"Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry."
Related Story: NPR
When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding limits on technology in the classroom.
But even as districts including Los Angeles Unified, Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.
In a post on X, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy.
A baffling move
Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.
She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google fended off in D.C.
Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search.
"The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court."
When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its original announcement, where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases.
NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether.
The "AI or nothing" approach
In any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs.
Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an "unacceptable risk" rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information.
The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina sued the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook.
Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois.
Related Story: NPR
"It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said.
Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI.
He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging.
"Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school."
The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well.
Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen
Google is a financial supporter of NPR.

articles.title: US government grounds all flights across the United States ‘due to extraordinary circumstances’
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday afternoon that it has grounded all flights across the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances” and issues related to safety.
The FAA’s website said the cause is an “equipment outage.” The site itself was down for a brief period at the time of publication, with a note that the website was “experiencing technical difficulties.”
Per an alert sent by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC, the FAA said the ground stop means that aircraft cannot take off from departure gates. The message said that the disruption was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” but did not specify further. The alert was not visible on the ATCSCC website at press time.
The alert stated that all departing flights must remain on the ground “until further notice.” Inbound international flights will be “managed on a case-by-case basis,” it said.
A spokesperson for the FAA told TechCrunch that it issued the ground stop “following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” which manage the airspace across the United States.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a post on X: “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”
It’s not clear what caused the ongoing FAA equipment outage. The outage comes in the same week that the administration rolled out an AI-powered tool for air traffic controllers to save aircraft flight time and fuel costs — though it’s unclear if the ongoing outage is related.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that there is “no indication yet that this was a nefarious act,” but warned that the recovery “is going to take some time.”
Updated with comment from the FAA, and remarks from Homeland Security.

articles.title: US Seizes $1.2 Billion In Crypto Stolen From Binance
articles.body:
US Seizes $1.2 Billion In Crypto Stolen From Binance (cnbc.com) 17
			
		 	
				U.S. authorities have seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen during Binance's $6 billion October hack, which the FBI attributes to North Korean military-linked hackers known as "TraderTraitor." The DOJ also said it disrupted infrastructure behind the "FaceStealer" deepfake scam, blamed for stealing more than $400 million in cryptocurrency. CNBC reports:  Collective efforts between the U.S. government and private sector have resulted in more than $2.7 billion of that amount being frozen. [...] The DOJ said it was taking coordinated action against what it called the North Korean government's "schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency." That includes "the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance," it said. DOJ units, law enforcement partners and virtual asset service providers have been working to intercept the stolen assets. But efforts to track and freeze the assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder them through various cryptocurrency channels.
Authorities have also seized cloud-based infrastructure used in a massive identity impersonation scam known as "FaceStealer," which has seen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen over 18 months, the DOJ said. The scheme sees hackers set up fake video meetings using stolen accounts and recordings of people known to the target by using AI-generated deepfakes. The hackers then say a technical problem requires a fix, install malware on a computer and take over the victim's communications, steal their cryptocurrency and target their contacts -- sometimes months or more than a year after the initial compromise.

articles.title: Security Agencies Worldwide Found to Use Ad-Based Surveillance System
articles.body:
Security Agencies Worldwide Found to Use Ad-Based Surveillance System
An investigation by Bloomberg into Penlink’s ad-based surveillance system Webloc builds off Citizen Lab research, identifying additional customers of the tracking technology. The findings that Webloc has been acquired by security agencies in a number of countries aligns with potential customers we identified in our April report.
Senior researcher Wolfie Christl notes that Webloc “is a powerful mass surveillance tool that’s trickling down from military and intelligence agencies to federal law enforcement and then to state and local police.”
Our report used open source research, freedom of information requests, and server infrastructure mapping to identify Webloc customers in the US, El Salvador, and Hungary. Since then, the Austrian Ministry of the Interior has also been confirmed as a customer. The Bloomberg investigation identified customers in additional countries including the UK, Netherlands, Germany, Mexico, Singapore, Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Israel.
The lawfulness of using these systems in Europe and the UK is highly controversial. While intrusive and disproportionate ad-based mass surveillance is problematic everywhere, its use in authoritarian countries identified by reporting is particularly dangerous.

articles.title: Mississippi Picked Another Senator
articles.body:
While most of the results of last Tuesday’s elections are now official, some are still being finalized.1 It’s been less than 48 hours since Mississippi’s Senate race was finally called for Democrat Scott Colom. On the other hand, it’s been a couple weeks since I first saw his incredibly viral campaign ad.2
Friend-of-the-site Daniel J. pointed me to this interview with Ryan Sayles, the 27-year-old Mississippi content creator behind the ad.
You know, [I] just added the entertainment or funny pieces of it, like emphasizing the way he said the words and stuff like that. And then I shot it, edited it, and added the music to it.
I sat there and edited for like five hours. I’ve heard that man say “shit” a million times.
Me too, Ryan. Me too.3
Footnotes:
- Alaska has decent reasons for taking so long in a tight race, as the Division of Elections explained: Alright, fine, fine. We can wait. ↩︎
- The video is archived here. ↩︎
- Politico’s summary quotes the ad like so: “Pick another protein? Shiiii-, I’d rather pick another senator instead.” I think that’s incorrect. I distinctly hear a “t” in there, for the full expletive. It sounds like Sayles agrees. ↩︎

articles.title: Sweet Potato Recipes
articles.body:
You gotta love a vegetable that can sit next to a burger as fries and then turn up in pie for dessert! Sweet potatoes are so much more than a Thanksgiving side, and they earn their place in my kitchen all year long. You can roast them until caramelized, blend them into silky soup, or use them to stretch a skillet dinner a little further. I’ve gathered 13 easy sweet potato recipes that put this affordable, filling ingredient to work, with a few holiday favorites for good measure! If you’ve got regular potatoes to use up, don’t miss our potato recipes roundup for even more ideas.
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
Classic Sweet Potato Recipes
Some days I want to make something cozy from scratch; other days, I want dinner to involve little more than a sheet pan and some salt. These classics cover both, with creamy soup, simple baked potatoes, fries, and a few sweeter options in the mix.
1. Baked Sweet Potatoes
Baked Sweet Potatoes
Sometimes, butter, salt, and pepper are all a baked sweet potato needs. But I also love how easy it is to dress one up with black beans, leftover chili, or whatever needs using in the fridge. They’re filling, inexpensive, and take just five minutes of hands-on prep. Short on time? Partially cooking them in the microwave before baking can cut the oven time down considerably.
2. Sweet Potato Soup
Creamy Sweet Potato Soup
I’m all for a quick stovetop soup, but roasting the sweet potatoes first is worth the extra step in this creamy sweet potato soup. It brings out their natural sweetness, which pairs well with the cumin, smoked paprika, cinnamon, and a little cayenne. Everything gets blended until silky smooth and finished with a splash of heavy cream (coconut milk works too!). At around $1.47 per serving, this is some seriously affordable comfort food.
3. Roasted Sweet Potatoes
Roasted Sweet Potatoes
Three ingredients and a hot sheet pan. That’s all you need for these beautifully caramelized roasted sweet potatoes! I preheat the baking sheet to give the cubes a head start on browning, then roast them until the edges are golden and the centers are soft and creamy. No parboiling, no complicated seasonings, and just $0.66 per serving. They’re delicious straight from the oven, but I also like adding leftovers to salads and grain bowls.
4. Air Fryer Sweet Potato Fries
Air Fryer Sweet Potato Fries
I always appreciate a side dish that only needs a few ingredients and doesn’t take over the oven. These air fryer sweet potato fries are tossed with olive oil and Creole seasoning for a sweet, salty, slightly spicy flavor that goes really well with burgers and sandwiches. They’re thicker and more tender than traditional fries rather than super crispy, but that makes them especially good for dipping into a little creamy comeback sauce.
5. Twice-Baked Sweet Potatoes
Twice Baked Sweet Potatoes
A regular baked sweet potato is delicious, but sometimes you want to dress things up a little. For these twice-baked sweet potatoes, scoop out the fluffy insides and mash them with butter, brown sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, and vanilla before putting them back in their skins and topping with marshmallows and homemade candied pecans. My advice? Make the pecans ahead so there’s one less thing to do when you’re ready to serve.
6. Sweet Potato Hash
Sweet Potato Hash
This sweet potato hash brings together diced sweet potatoes, savory breakfast sausage, peppers, and onions in one hearty skillet. It’s delicious with a fried egg on top, but there’s plenty here to make a satisfying breakfast or brunch on its own. You get six servings from one skillet, making this a handy recipe for feeding a crowd or getting ahead on breakfasts for the week.
Hearty and Budget-Friendly Dinners
Sweet potatoes make a very convincing case for stretching dinner, especially when they’re paired with beans, pasta, or ground meat. These three meals have enough going on to stand alone, with plenty of savory spices to balance out the potatoes’ natural sweetness.
7. Sweet Potato Ground Turkey Skillet
Sweet Potato and Ground Turkey Skillet
Ground turkey gets a serious flavor upgrade in this sweet potato and ground turkey skillet! Thyme, sage, and smoked paprika season the turkey and vegetables, while orzo cooks right in the same pan, soaking up the flavorful broth. A handful of kale and some Parmesan finish things off, giving you four generous servings in about 40 minutes. I particularly appreciate that the pasta cooks alongside everything else (saving another pot from the washing up!)
8. Sweet Potato Black Bean Skillet
Sweet Potato Black Bean Skillet
This sweet potato black bean skillet is a hearty, naturally vegan dinner that comes together in about 25 minutes. The sweet potatoes are browned in the skillet to bring out their natural sweetness, then combined with black beans, bell pepper, kale, tomatoes, and a smoky blend of spices. I like serving this over rice to make it even more filling, and the leftovers are ideal for meal prep!
9. Sweet Potato Chili
Chorizo Sweet Potato Chili
There’s a very good reason this sweet potato chili doesn’t need a long list of seasonings. Mexican chorizo already brings plenty of smoky, spicy flavor to the pot! Tender sweet potatoes balance that heat, while inexpensive canned beans help turn it into six filling servings on a budget. Add your favorite chili toppings, grab some tortilla chips, and dinner is sorted. Leftovers freeze well, too.
Thanksgiving Sweet Potato Favorites
I have a soft spot for the classics at Thanksgiving, and sweet potatoes are responsible for some of the best ones. This little lineup includes a crunchy-topped casserole, a creamy homemade pie, and two delicious breads worth making room for. Better still, they all use familiar ingredients and won’t send your holiday grocery bill through the roof.
10. Sweet Potato Casserole
Sweet Potato Casserole
I’m not saying a crunchy pecan streusel is better than marshmallows, but it makes a pretty strong case! Underneath that buttery topping, this sweet potato casserole has a fluffy, lightly spiced filling made with mashed sweet potatoes, cinnamon, vanilla, and brown sugar. It makes eight servings for less than a dollar each, which is pretty impressive for a classic Thanksgiving side dish. And you only need about 40 minutes from start to finish!
11. Sweet Potato Pie
Sweet Potato Pie
If you’re looking for an affordable homemade dessert to finish your Thanksgiving meal, don’t overlook sweet potato pie. Baking the sweet potatoes first gives the creamy custard filling a deeper, slightly caramelized flavor, while cinnamon, nutmeg, and vanilla add that familiar holiday warmth. A store-bought pie crust keeps things manageable, and you can make the whole pie ahead of time to free up the oven on Thanksgiving Day.
12. Sweet Potato Cornbread
Sweet Potato Cornbread
A hot cast-iron skillet gives this sweet potato cornbread a beautifully browned crust, while mashed sweet potatoes and sour cream keep the inside rich and moist. It’s thicker and a little sweeter than everyday cornbread, with cinnamon and nutmeg adding just enough warmth without turning it into cake. I think it’s especially delicious served warm with butter.
13. Sweet Potato Biscuits
Sweet Potato Biscuits
I can make a pretty convincing argument for serving homemade biscuits at any meal, but especially Thanksgiving! Adding mashed sweet potato to the dough gives these sweet potato biscuits a lovely orange color, a subtle sweetness, and a wonderfully soft & tender texture. You can even microwave the sweet potato to save time!
More Great Recipe Roundups
Our Sweet Potato round up was originally published 9/29/23. It was retested, reworked, and republished to be better than ever 11/15/26.

articles.title: Elephants found to be increasingly isolated leading to fractured social networks
articles.body:
Elephants Found to be Increasingly Isolated, Leading to Fractured Social Networks
With a troubling decline in the population, researchers warn of a tipping point for the highly social animals
Published Date
Article Content
Key Takeaways
- UC San Diego researchers studied the social dynamics of hundreds of Asian elephants over more than a decade in Sri Lanka.
- They tracked a decrease in the population of the highly social animals that has led to fractured and more isolated communities.
- Surpassing a social “tipping point,” they warn, can be detrimental to the future of the animals.
Humans and many other social animals thrive in well-established community networks. Asian elephants are one example of a species that flourishes in groups that work together to access food and care for their young, among other social bonds.
University of California San Diego scientists in the School of Biological Sciences studying the intricacies of Asian elephant community structures have documented a troubling downturn in the population of the animals resulting in fractured social communities. Their study is published on the cover of the November 12 issue of Science.
Analyzing the social dynamics of more than 440 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years at the Udawalawe National Park in Sri Lanka, the researchers studied key shifts in the demographics of the elephants that seemed to trigger social communities becoming smaller and more isolated.
“We found that gradual accumulation of losses from turnover preceded sudden change in the social networks among females in a wild population of Asian elephants,” the researchers explained in the study, which was led by Postdoctoral Researcher Anastasia Madsen from the laboratory of Associate Professor Shermin de Silva in the Department of Ecology, Behavior and Evolution. de Silva also serves as president and founder of the conservation nonprofit Trunks & Leaves Inc.
The researchers’ analysis indicates a social structure tipping point. As the number of elephants in the population decreased over time, due to a combination of likely deaths, permanent emigrations of elephants and fewer incoming individuals, the population as a whole appears to have crossed a critical threshold that resulted in a shift from large, densely connected social communities, to smaller and less-connected social groupings.
“We see individual elephants leaving and possibly dying at accelerating rates, but new individuals are not coming into the population,” said Madsen. “With fewer individuals in the population, those who are left will naturally have fewer relationships. However, the remaining elephants are also changing their relationships with each other.”
This new dynamic is a cause for concern, says Madsen, since the animals leverage their social groups and connections to forage, acquire information and raise young.
“We can probably all relate to the feeling of social isolation brought about, paradoxically, with the advent of digital communications that seem to remove the physical constraints of needing to be in the same place at the same time,” said de Silva. “But for many social species, which includes ourselves as much as elephants, we have to remember that social connectivity is very much a matter of sharing space and building relationships throughout our lives. Crucially, in order to have resilient communities, we need to be able to replace the relationships that are lost over time.”
Many elephant populations are already impacted through deaths resulting from poaching and conflicts with humans. Other contributing factors may be disruptions in habitat connectivity and less food available for the elephants as ecological conditions change across the 119-square-mile park and surroundings.
The new social fracturing structure observed by the scientists may not be easily repaired, the researchers warn.
“In general, we need to be more aware of these types of tipping points where we see sudden shifts after changes have been slowly building up,” said Madsen. “Once we move past the tipping point, it’s much harder to go back to previous states.”
The new findings will serve future studies seeking to understand shifts in animal society structures, how to detect such tranformations and the factors responsible for vulnerabilities. The study also stimulates ongoing discussions for conserving elephant populations as humans expand into areas where elephants historically thrived.
“We are gaining more evidence that studying social patterns is an important tool for us to see when things are going wrong in natural populations and, hopefully, to be able to do something about it,” said Madsen.
The researchers of the study were: Anastasia E. Madsen, T.V. Pushpakumara, U. Sameera Weerathunga, Devaka K. Weerakoon and Shermin de Silva.
Funding for the research was provided by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Asian Elephant Conservation Grants (F11AP00258, F14AP00256 and F17AP00308); National Science Foundation (grant DBI-2305860); University of Pennsylvania; UC San Diego; and Trunks & Leaves Inc.

articles.title: Lego's BrickLink Marketplace Back Online After Week-Long Outage Caused By 'Cyber Incident'
articles.body:
Lego's BrickLink Marketplace Back Online After Week-Long Outage Caused By 'Cyber Incident' (brickfanatics.com) 4
			
		 	
				LEGO's BrickLink marketplace is back online after a week-long outage caused by what the company described as a "cyber incident," during which an unauthorized third party accessed some user data. Details about exactly what data was accessed remain unclear. The site went offline on November 5 and remained unavailable until November 12, preventing users from buying or selling LEGO sets and parts during the busy holiday shopping season. According to Brick Fanatics, LEGO initially described the outage as "necessary work" before confirming that the platform had suffered a security incident.
In an email to users, LEGO acknowledged that "some of the information associated with your account was accessed and disclosed by an unauthorized party," including potentially usernames and IP addresses. However, the company insisted that "your password, postal address, and financial information were not disclosed." Those assurances have since come under scrutiny following reports of convincing phishing emails containing detailed personal and purchase information.
The outage also dealt a significant blow to independent sellers who rely on BrickLink for income. Simon Webster, who operates stores on both BrickLink and rival marketplace Brick Owl, reported that his overall sales revenue fell 52% over a four-day period, even as sales through Brick Owl rose 79%. "Their comms are amateur at the best of times, but surely they should be able to send an email to let sellers and buyers alike know what is happening and what they're doing to rectify it," Webster said. "But no, we're all left in the dark."
The incident has renewed concerns about BrickLink's aging infrastructure. Founded in 2000 and acquired by LEGO in 2019, the marketplace reportedly runs on a complex collection of interconnected systems that makes modernization difficult. The Brick Fanatics report questions whether the 25-year-old platform remains fit for purpose and whether prolonged outages and security concerns could push sellers toward competing marketplaces like Brick Owl.

articles.title: Parents and Teachers Decry Google Pledge To Yank Search If Schools Block AI
articles.body:
Parents and Teachers Decry Google Pledge To Yank Search If Schools Block AI (theguardian.com) 57
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Parents and teachers across the US are criticizing Google's announcement that schools choosing to block AI tools could also lose access to Google Search. Google announced last week a range of new AI tools for schools and classrooms, alongside options allowing teachers and administrators to restrict their use. The company said schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom, but that schools that choose to block Google's AI tools will also lose access to its search engine. [...] Parents and teachers across the country raised concerns to the Guardian about AI's potential to weaken students' critical-thinking skills and the growing influence of big tech in education. Some called on schools to consider alternative search engines, while others argued that students should be taught how to use AI responsibly rather than prevented from accessing it altogether.
Jen Atay, a 51-year-old teacher in Hawaii, lambasted Google's approach, saying: "When the software is free, you are the product, and it is inappropriate for Google to test or develop AI with minors. This should not be allowed at all." A 44-year-old father of two boys in Amissville, Virginia, said he worries that "AI will weaken people's ability to think critically. I use AI in my work, but it would not be effective if I did not have well over a decade of experience under my belt. Even the best models are often flat-out wrong in their responses." [...] Others questioned why schools should depend on Google at all.  An 84-year-old retiree and mother in Maryland, said: "Google decided to follow the evil path to riches. When they started, they were great. Today they are simply evil money grubbers  Schools should tell Google to go pound sand and simply have kids use DuckDuckGo or one of the other search engines  There is nothing Google offers that is not available from some other source." [...]
Not everyone believes blocking AI is the answer. Some argued that schools should focus on teaching students how to use the technology responsibly. A 67-year-old emerging technology teacher in Texas said: "I do not blame Google. AI is not going away. I've been very frustrated this year trying to teach AI literacy with AI blocked. Schools need to teach how to properly use AI, not block it." A California resident echoed that view, arguing that schools could use Google's AI tools to teach students to question the information they receive. "Google Search has existed since the 90s and it's crazy of them to completely remove it instead of just removing Gemini. That being said, I would like to see schools actually permit the use of Gemini and use it as an opportunity to show students how its sources aren't always valid and you can't trust everything an AI tells you," they said.

articles.title: Crustless Quiche
articles.body:
Crustless Quiche
This crustless quiche recipe offers the tender texture that you love in a regular quiche. It's an easy, healthy, high-protein egg dish!
Posted by Kathryne Taylor on November 13, 2026
Craving quiche, but don’t want to fuss with a crust? This eggy wonder is perfectly tender inside, like a regular quiche! You’d never guess it, but there’s cottage cheese inside, which makes it nice and soft, similar to egg bites. This protein-rich quiche recipe is the perfect way to balance morning muffins and breads.
If you’re particular about your eggs like I am, you’ll appreciate this recipe. It’s made differently from a baked frittata. While I love a well-made frittata (you can find all my tips here), this recipe is a safer bet. Even if you cook it a couple of minutes too long, it won’t turn brown on the bottom or spongy like a frittata can. Try it, and you’ll see!
How to Make a Quiche Without Crust
You’ll find the full recipe at the bottom of the post, but here’s why this recipe works so well.
1. Cottage cheese instead of milk or cream.
It’s the secret ingredient that offers a very subtle tang and extra protein. Once blended, the lumpy texture disappears, which explains why I’d never guess it was there. Quiche typically has a high milk-to-eggs ratio, and the cottage cheese helps the eggs firm up just right without spending a long time in the oven.
2. Baked in a water bath.
I promise, the water bath is easy to manage, and it makes all the difference. We’ll bake the egg dish on a rimmed baking sheet filled with a small amount of hot water. The steam from the water bath gives these bites a luscious, smooth texture by gently cooking the eggs, preventing them from rising so quickly that they develop big air bubbles. Without the water bath, the eggs would be firmer and brown at the bottom.
Watch how to make this recipe
Flavor Variations that Work
The ingredients shown here are inspired by traditional French quiche Florentine, which typically includes sautéed spinach with onion and Gruyère or Swiss cheese. You can’t go wrong with this classic combination. That said, you can easily change up the greens, onion and cheese:
- Instead of spinach, you could sauté chopped kale, chard or collard greens until tender (remove the tough ribs before cooking).
- Instead of yellow onion, you could use 1/4 cup chopped green onion.
- As for the cheese, anything goes. Cheddar, Parmesan or goat cheese would be lovely.
You can also add up to 1 cup tender or cooked vegetables, cut into bite-sized pieces. Try cooking bell pepper with your onions, or adding quartered cherry tomatoes.
Cheese Tip
Buy your own block of cheese and grate it before using. Pre-shredded and pre-crumbled cheeses are coated in cellulose powder, so they don’t melt as nicely.
Quiche Serving Suggestions
This easy, protein-rich quiche makes a great breakfast or brunch, but you could also make it for lunch or dinner. Here are my suggestions to build a full meal.
- For a simple occasion, round out your meal with crusty sourdough (toasted if you’d like) and a little green salad.
- For a full-blown spread, consider serving quiche with crispy hash browns or any of my pancake recipes, which you can cook on the stove while the quiche bakes in the oven. Or instead of pancakes, make muffins the day before.
- For a fun summer salad, try my Easy Tomato Salad or Summertime Fruit Salad. In the cooler months, try my French Carrot Salad or Favorite Green Salad with Apples, Cranberries and Pepitas.
Please let me know how your quiche turns out in the comments. I love hearing from you.
Crustless Quiche
This crustless quiche recipe offers the tender texture that you love in a regular quiche. It’s an easy, healthy, high-protein egg dish! This spinach, onion and cheese version was inspired by traditional quiche Florentine. Check the post for variations. Recipe yields 6 medium slices; you could likely bake two quiches in the oven at once.
Ingredients
- 8 large eggs
- 1 cup (8 ounces) cottage cheese (4% milkfat or higher, made with whole milk)
- ¼ teaspoon fine salt
- 10 twists of freshly ground black pepper
- 2 teaspoons unsalted butter, plus more for greasing the pan
- ½ cup chopped yellow onion
- 2 cups (3.5 ounces) finely chopped spinach
- 1 packed cup (4 ounces) freshly grated Gruyère or Swiss cheese
Instructions
- Preheat the oven to 325 degrees Fahrenheit, and grease a glass pie plate with butter. In a kettle or medium saucepan, bring 3 cups of water to a boil and maintain a simmer until it’s needed.
- In a blender, combine the eggs, cottage cheese, and the salt and pepper. Blend on high for 8 to 10 seconds, just until the mixture is smooth and frothy (no longer!). Set it aside.
- Melt the butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add the onion and a pinch of salt, and stir to combine. Cook until the onion is tender and translucent, about 3 to 5 minutes. Add the spinach, and cook until the spinach is wilted and reduced in volume, about 1 to 2 minutes. Remove the mixture from the heat and let it cool for a couple of minutes, then stir it into the blender mixture. Stir in half of the cheese.
- Place the prepared pie plate on a large, rimmed baking sheet. Carefully pour the egg mixture into the pie plate. Sprinkle the remaining cheese on top, then transfer the stacked pans to the oven. Carefully pour the hot water into the sheet pan, enough to submerge the bottom of the pie pan by at least ⅛ inch.
- Bake for 34 to 39 minutes, until the eggs are puffed and appear cooked, and the center of the quiche jiggles just a bit when you give it a gentle shimmy.
- Remove the pie plate from the sheet pan of water in the oven, and let it cool for at least 10 minutes on a cooling rack before serving. Leftover quiche will keep in the fridge, covered, for up to 4 days, or in the freezer for up to 3 months. Reheat slices in a microwave or on a rimmed baking sheet in a 300-degree oven until warmed through (they will release some moisture while reheating, which you can discard).
Nutrition
The information shown is an estimate provided by an online nutrition calculator. It should not be considered a substitute for a professional nutritionist’s advice. See our full nutrition disclosure here.

articles.title: Ggml v1.0.0
articles.body:
Repository navigation
Overview
ggml 1.0.0 prunes the deprecated public API and the legacy DIAG_MASK ops, adds configurable YaRN truncation and FP8 support, and brings broad performance work across backends: few-row quantized matmuls and MoE fusion on CUDA/Metal, a Vulkan prefill FlashAttention path, a device-side MoE scheduler on SYCL, decomposed Adreno FlashAttention in OpenCL, new WebGPU kernels, expanded Hexagon op coverage, and scheduler improvements that avoid uploading unused inputs.
API changes
- Pruned deprecated API and removed the legacy DIAG_MASK_INF/DIAG_MASK_ZERO ops, bumping the RPC protocol to reject incompatible peers (llama/29801, llama/31946)
- Added ggml_rope_set_truncate/ggml_rope_get_truncate to control YaRN correction-bound rounding (llama/30206, llama/30802)
- Implemented the backward pass for TRI (llama/30712)
- Added MUL_MAT src1 precision tests and gating for ggml_prec_set_acc (llama/31896, llama/31851)
- Bumped the RPC protocol to v9 with faster loading and graceful failure on unreachable endpoints or failed handshakes (llama/29413, llama/30415)
Core changes
- Scheduler skips uploading inputs that are not read and prefetches only inputs produced by earlier splits (llama/31419, llama/32100)
- MoE cache can compute a share of the cache misses on the CPU and copy the results back asynchronously (llama/30966)
- Meta backend raises the compute view limit for buffers with few tensors (llama/31447)
Backend changes
CUDA
- Added few-row MMQ for batch sizes 2-24 and MMVF for BF16 few-row matmuls (llama/31533, llama/31959)
- Added OCP FP8 support and fused NVFP4 gate/up matmuls with GLU in MMQ (llama/28413, llama/31296)
- Extended FlashAttention with an sm70 head-size-256 config and MMA head sizes 40/72 (llama/27997, llama/30285)
- Improved graph handling: skip compat checks on reuse, re-instantiate on cluster-dim changes, move graph state (llama/32004, llama/31284, llama/32001)
- MoE: skip empty MMQ stream-k tiles, linearize the MoE layout, and sanitize post-bias NaNs (llama/32067, llama/31047, llama/31005)
- Added a debug buffer pool and halved the VMM pool reservation with reserve retries (llama/31919, llama/30542)
- HIP: use a fixed BLAS workspace and add an MFMA lightning indexer for CDNA2 (llama/31838, llama/29050)
- Added a d_state=64 SSM_SCAN fast path and made radix Top-K deterministic for ties (llama/31818, llama/31084)
Metal
- Fused MoE routing and kept fusable node groups inside a single command buffer (llama/31615, llama/31688)
- Made radix Top-K deterministic for ties, added mul_mm for 32<=K<64, and switched TRI to select (llama/31084, llama/30982, llama/30711)
- Fixed GROUP_NORM for ne03>1 and out-of-bounds accesses in the FA output and SOLVE_TRI kernels (llama/31852, llama/31662, llama/32103)
Vulkan
- Added an Intel FlashAttention prefill kernel (llama/29357)
- Added batched tensor copies, a test-fusion interface, and ReBAR detection (llama/31418, llama/30769, llama/31658)
- Enabled dequantized KV with CM2, YaRN truncation, RDNA3/4 large-tile split-K, and large coopmat matmul on newer AMD drivers (llama/31526, llama/30802, llama/30280, llama/31587)
- Added a tiled-transpose concat shader and FWHT kernels for block widths above 512 (llama/30591, llama/29772)
- Fixed MoltenVK out-of-bounds accesses, GROUP_NORM workgroup limits, and FA scratch sizing (llama/31890, llama/31930, llama/30487)
- Capped scalar FlashAttention at 8 rows for large heads on Qualcomm (llama/30829)
SYCL
- Added a device-side MoE scheduler (llama/30156)
- Made the oneDNN FA cache thread-safe and un-gated fused SDPA for Alchemist at head_dim=64 (llama/31138, llama/31574)
- Cached the device id and reject buffers that would exceed VRAM (llama/31126, llama/32013, llama/31285)
- Added exact rounding for CPY to Q4_1/Q5_1/Q8_0, strided CLAMP, and f16 SWIGLU_OAI (llama/31465, llama/31784, llama/30857)
- Fixed AOT for allocations above 4GB (llama/31873)
OpenCL
- Added decomposed Adreno FlashAttention and improved decode performance (llama/32046, llama/31633)
- Added q6_k tiled, q8_0, and f32/q5_k multi-column GEMV kernels and f32 MUL_MAT_ID (llama/31758, llama/30947, llama/31783)
- Added arange, non-contiguous sigmoid, repeat for f16/i32/i16/bf16, and DSV4 HC pre/post kernels (llama/31829, llama/31687, llama/31782, llama/31623)
- Enabled multi-column GEMV by default for Adreno X2 (llama/31694)
WebGPU
- Added batched tensor API support and returned maxBufferSize from get_max_size (llama/31473, llama/31348)
- Added GROUP_NORM, MEAN, COUNT_EQUAL, and PAD_REFLECT_1D kernels (llama/31490, llama/31591, llama/31578, llama/31877)
- Supported the YaRN truncation config (llama/30802)
Hexagon
- Added Q5_0/Q5_1 support and optimized conv_2d while adding conv_3d (llama/32094, llama/31814)
- Fused post-norm residual add into RMS_NORM_MUL and added set_tensor_n (llama/31822, llama/31744)
- Added automatic libhtp loading and fixed 64-bit FastRPC handle truncation (llama/31781, llama/30952)
- Fixed the host build with clang-cl on Windows ARM64 (llama/32011)
CPU
- Switched MUL_MAT to F32 src1 and accumulate FlashAttention V in F32 (llama/31854, llama/29810)
- Added SpacemiT GATED_DELTA_NET RVV and Q4_1 32x256 HP kernels and enabled IME2 MXFP4 repack (llama/31897, llama/31929, llama/31776)
- Enabled the 4x4 simd_gemm tile on ARM NEON and added bf16/q8_0 VXE to llamafile (llama/32128, llama/31866)
CANN
- Fail early when a buffer type is unsupported (llama/31270)
ZDNN
- Accept non-zdnn tensors, invalidate compute tensors after each op, and fix release backend lib detection (llama/31824, llama/31905)
OpenVINO
- Supported the YaRN truncation config (llama/30802)
More info

articles.title: GigChain Keys – a free, open-source MainStage alternative
articles.body:
Download · Getting started · User guide · Get help · What's new · Discord · ♥ Sponsor
GigChain Keys is a live-performance host for keyboard players, in the spirit of MainStage and Gig Performer. It plays the VST3 and VST2 instruments and effects already on your computer, keeps every song of the night in a setlist with its own sounds, shows each song's chords and lyrics big enough to read from the keys, and turns those chords into notes falling onto a keyboard so you can practise them.
It is free, with no adverts, no licence keys and no nag screens. It is open source too, under the GPL.
Important
Public alpha: testers wanted. GigChain Keys is in early testing. It works and is played on real rigs, but it has not yet met the wide range of computers, audio interfaces, keyboards and plugins out there. Features and setlist files may still change between versions, and you may meet bugs. Please try it at home and in rehearsal before trusting it on a gig, keep copies of your setlists, and tell us what works and what breaks. Your feedback decides what gets fixed and built next.
All versions, with their release notes, are on the Releases page.
During the alpha, the Windows installer and the macOS app are not
code-signed. Code-signing certificates carry a yearly cost, and they will
be added as the project grows and community interest and
sponsorship make that possible. Until then, Windows
and macOS show a one-time warning on first start; the steps below get past
it. The builds are made from the source in this repository by its public
build scripts, and every release lists the SHA-256 checksum of each file
(SHA256SUMS.txt), so you can check your download is the genuine one:
Get-FileHash .\GigChainKeys-0.1.0-x64-setup.exe -Algorithm SHA256   # Windows (PowerShell)shasum -a 256 GigChainKeys-0.1.0-arm64.dmg                          # macOS (Terminal)
sha256sum GigChainKeys-0.6.0-x86_64.AppImage                         # Linux
AppImage: make it executable, then run it (or double-click it in your file manager):
chmod +x GigChainKeys-*-x86_64.AppImage
./GigChainKeys-*-x86_64.AppImage
(If it says "FUSE" is missing, install libfuse2, or run it with
--appimage-extract-and-run.)
.deb: sudo apt install ./gigchain-keys_*_amd64.deb, then start
GigChain Keys from your menu or type gigchain-keys. Remove it with
sudo apt remove gigchain-keys.
Sound goes through PulseAudio or PipeWire (or JACK, chosen in Settings;
on PipeWire, start the app with pw-jack to use JACK);
Linux VST3 plugins are found in ~/.vst3 and /usr/lib/vst3. The AppImage
uses your system's sound libraries: if it says libjack.so.0 is missing,
install libjack-jackd2-0 (the .deb installs it for you).
Windows SmartScreen may say "Windows protected your PC". Click More info, then Run anyway. This happens once.
The app is not notarized by Apple yet. Open the disk image, drag GigChain Keys to Applications, and open it once. When macOS refuses, go to System Settings → Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway.
- Instruments: four come built in (Saw Stack Pro, Piano Pro, Pads Pro and the SoundFont Player, below), and any VST3 or VST2 instruments and effects play too. GigChain Keys finds them in the usual plugin folders by itself. Want more? These free ones cover pianos, synths and pads: The app shows the same list (Help > Get free instruments). They are the makers' own downloads, not part of GigChain Keys.
- A MIDI keyboard (USB or a MIDI interface). A sustain pedal, knobs and pads are used when present.
- An audio interface is recommended for low latency (ASIO on Windows). Your computer's own sound works too.
  
  
Perform: the song plays along its parts; Next part and Loop part land on the bar line.
  
  
Right-click a fader, a pan knob or the master: MIDI Learn, then turn a knob on your keyboard.
  
  
  
Warm-ups: the finger for every note, then the score.
- Download and install GigChain Keys, then start it.
- Open Settings (top right) and choose your audio device and MIDI keyboard.
- Click New setlist, then + Song.
- Open the Instruments tab on the left and double-click an instrument. Play!
- Paste the song's chords into the Chart tab, then try Perform and Practice.
The Getting started page walks through it step by step. Inside the app, press F1 (or click Help) at any time.
Short videos, each showing one part of GigChain Keys (all of them):
- The overview: the whole app, start to finish
- Loop station · Chord charts and lyrics · The 10-minute warm-up
- Layers, splits and effects · Sounds on your pads
- Saw Stack Pro, the EDM synth · Piano Pro, the EDM piano
The user guide is built into the app (Help → User guide, or F1) and is also here on GitHub:
- Something not working? Start with Troubleshooting.
- Found a bug? Report it. The support page says what to include (and where the log file is).
- Have an idea? Suggest a feature.
- A security problem? Please report it privately: see SECURITY.md.
- Want to talk to other players? Join the Discord.
Come and join the Discord: ask how to set up a sound, share your rig and your setlists, tell us what's missing for your gigs, or just hang out with other keys players. If you know someone who'd use GigChain Keys, send them the link.
GigChain Keys is free and stays free: no adverts, no paid version, no keys. If it helps your gigs, a donation keeps it going. It pays for the time to fix and build things, and the first goal is code-signing certificates, so Windows and macOS install GigChain Keys without a warning.
One-off or monthly, any amount, through GitHub Sponsors. Thank you!
GigChain Keys uses numbered versions. Each release lists what is new and what was fixed in the changelog and on the Releases page.
What is coming next is in the roadmap: bundled free instruments, a tablet remote for the music stand, melody and intro practice, and more.
GigChain Keys is written in C++20 with Qt 6 (QML) and hosts plugins with the Steinberg VST3 SDK; audio and MIDI go through RtAudio and RtMidi.
- Building from source: Windows, Linux and macOS
- Contributing: how to send a fix, and the code rules
- Releasing: how a version is built and published
- Roadmap: what is coming next
Everyone taking part is expected to follow the code of conduct.
- riversongswgs-glitch: testing the releases and reporting with videos and logs, which shaped the Flow bar, Practice in time with the click, chord lengths, the big count-in and the chart editor's fixes
GigChain Keys is free software: you can share and change it under the terms of the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later (LICENSE).
It is built with:
- Qt (LGPL-3.0)
- the Steinberg VST3 SDK (MIT)
- the Steinberg ASIO SDK (GPL-3.0)
- RtAudio and RtMidi (MIT-style)
- FluidSynth (LGPL-2.1-or-later), which plays SoundFonts in the SoundFont Player
- effects ported from Vital (GPL-3.0) in Saw Stack Pro and Piano Pro
- Piano Pro's concert grand: Alexander Holm's Salamander Grand Piano (CC BY 3.0); its upright from Versilian Studios' VCSL (CC0); its Rhodes: Jeff Learman's jRhodes3d (samples CC BY-NC 4.0); its Wurlitzer, CP80 and Pianet: Greg Sullivan's E-Pianos (CC BY 3.0)
- Pads Pro's string section from Versilian Studios' VSCO 2 CE (CC0) and its piano from the Splendid Grand Piano (public domain)
The full notices ship with the app (THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt).
VST is a registered trademark of Steinberg Media Technologies GmbH. ASIO is a trademark of Steinberg Media Technologies GmbH. MainStage, Logic, Gig Performer, Kickstart, Korg M1, Rhodes and DX7 are trademarks of their owners; GigChain Keys is not affiliated with them.

articles.title: Hawaii DOT: All West Coast flights halted by SpaceX debris after FAA ground stop
articles.body:
FAA lifts nationwide ground stop: What Hawaii travelers should know
Travelers should continue checking with their carriers.
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - A nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that disrupted several domestic flights to and from Hawaiʻi was lifted at around 3:20 p.m. Friday.
The Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation said in an update that both the nationwide ground stop and a temporary pause for space debris had been lifted.
Delays may continue as airlines accommodate passengers from earlier flights, officials said.
RELATED POST: Flights halted at airports across US due to air traffic control communications problems, FAA says
Initial ground stop affected domestic travel
The FAA issued the ground stop following a communications issue affecting air traffic control centers. Flight disruptions had been intermittent with restrictions changing throughout the day.
Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation Director Ed Sniffen said officials were notified of the ground stop at about 10:50 a.m. for domestic flights to and from the continental U.S.
Interisland flights were not affected, he said.
“There’s been adjustments throughout. Initially, flights, international flights were unrestricted. Then we got notifications that there are some conflicts with the international flights,” Sniffen said.
At around 12:30 p.m., Sniffen said some flights had been cleared to leave Hawaiʻi for the West Coast.
Officials were repositioning aircraft and planning to use taxiways and some runways for parking to make room for arriving planes, he said.
SpaceX debris halted flights again
In a 1:55 p.m. update, the DOT announced all West Coast flights had been halted due to debris from a SpaceX launch.
SpaceX launched its Starship rocket from Texas on Friday, but its first-stage booster malfunctioned and ended up in the Gulf after an automatic abort, according to The Associated Press. The spacecraft continued toward orbit.
“The big message to all the public is things are changing pretty quickly,” Sniffen said. “Before you come down to the airport, make sure you reach out to your carrier.”
11/13/26 1:55PM: All west coast flights have been halted due to debris from SpaceX launch. Please continue to check with your carrier for further updates. https://t.co/Et1gtFbfe7
— Hawaii DOT (@DOTHawaii) November 13, 2026
What travelers should know
Hawaiian and Alaska airlines said a flexible travel policy was in place for guests who need to change their plans.
The airlines said it would take time to safely return operations to schedule after the ground stop was lifted.
Nationwide ground stops are rare. A pilot notification system outage prompted one in January 2023; the previous nationwide stop followed the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

articles.title: Anthropic Upgrades Claude Code Projects to Run Parallel AI Workers Hands-Free
articles.body:
Anthropic Upgrades Claude Code Projects to Run Parallel AI Workers Hands-Free
Anthropic ships a proactive coordinator, shareable read-only threads, reminders, and /btw and /fork slash commands to Claude Code Projects.
- Claude Code Projects coordinator is now proactive, answering questions and pushing thread status updates in chat.
- Individual threads can be shared as read-only links to signed-in Claude users; threads with local computer access are excluded.
- Reminders let a thread hide itself and resurface in the project chat at a scheduled time.
- /btw opens a side thread for tangents; /fork branches a new thread from the current one.
- Threads panel adds a recents row and artifact thumbnails for easier retrieval across large projects.
- Public beta on Pro and Max across web, desktop, and the latest mobile app; Team and Enterprise excluded.
Anthropic has updated Claude Code Projects with proactive coordinator messages, read-only thread sharing, reminders, branching commands, and improved artifact navigation. The changes reduce the monitoring required when several cloud sessions work in parallel.
Each project is a long-running conversation with a coordinator that assigns work to threads. Every thread runs as an independent Claude Code cloud session with its own repository copy and Git branch. The coordinator directs the project from thread reports, while overlapping code changes surface as standard Git merge conflicts when branches are combined.
The coordinator reports without prompting
The coordinator now answers questions directly in project chat and posts status updates as threads progress. Previously, developers had to monitor the thread list to find sessions waiting for input. The updated behavior brings pending decisions, completed tasks, and blocked work into the main conversation.
Read-only links stop at local access
Individual threads can now be shared through read-only links with anyone signed in to Claude. A developer can open the thread menu, select Share, and send the generated URL without exposing the rest of the project.
Threads that accessed a local computer remain unshareable. The restriction prevents shared transcripts from exposing local file contents, shell output, or other machine data gathered during the session.
Park a thread or branch the work
The two slash commands were already available in regular Claude Code sessions. Their addition to Projects brings the same branching workflow to coordinated, multi-thread work.
Artifacts surface sooner
The threads panel now places recently opened, updated, and pinned threads in a row at the top. Each thread can also display thumbnails for generated documents, diagrams, and other artifacts, with the previews controlled through view settings.
The redesign simplifies project settings and local-folder access as well. Anthropic has released the changes on the web, desktop clients, and the latest mobile app.
Parallelism draws from the same allowance
Anthropic introduced the public beta on September 17 for Pro and Max subscribers who joined the waitlist. Team and Enterprise plans remain unsupported. Eligible subscribers who lack access can still join the waitlist.
Projects carry no separate fee, but every worker consumes the subscriber’s existing Claude Code allowance. Anthropic limits accounts to 200 new threads per day across all projects. A thread that reaches a usage limit pauses and resumes automatically when capacity becomes available.
Project usage appears separately in the usage controls, and developers can choose the model and effort level for the coordinator and worker threads. New projects default to Opus for both roles, with low effort for the coordinator and high effort for workers. Several high-effort sessions running at once can exhaust plan limits faster than a single Claude Code session.
Where many threads pay off
Projects fit engineering work that can be divided into independent tasks and reconciled through branches and pull requests. Anthropic’s examples include:
- Performance work: Assign separate threads to profile endpoints, test optimizations, and open pull requests. A target such as p75 checkout latency refers to the response time at or below which 75% of requests finish.
- Cross-repository migrations: Connect API, web, and mobile repositories, then create one thread per codebase and report the required merge order.
- Batch changes: Distribute refactors, dependency upgrades, test repairs, or bug-triage items across parallel sessions.
Tasks with strict dependencies still require developers to sequence pull requests and resolve conflicts. Projects also remain cloud-only and limited to Claude Code, while parallel workers draw from the same plan limits. Small changes that fit one branch and one context window generally consume fewer resources in a regular Claude Code session.

The coordinator now answers questions directly in project chat and posts status updates as threads progress. Previously, developers had to monitor the thread list to find sessions waiting for input. The updated behavior brings pending decisions, completed tasks, and blocked work into the main conversation.
Read-only links stop at local access
Individual threads can now be shared through read-only links with anyone signed in to Claude. A developer can open the thread menu, select Share, and send the generated URL without exposing the rest of the project.
Threads that accessed a local computer remain unshareable. The restriction prevents shared transcripts from exposing local file contents, shell output, or other machine data gathered during the session.
Park a thread or branch the work
The two slash commands were already available in regular Claude Code sessions. Their addition to Projects brings the same branching workflow to coordinated, multi-thread work.
Artifacts surface sooner
The threads panel now places recently opened, updated, and pinned threads in a row at the top. Each thread can also display thumbnails for generated documents, diagrams, and other artifacts, with the previews controlled through view settings.
The redesign simplifies project settings and local-folder access as well. Anthropic has released the changes on the web, desktop clients, and the latest mobile app.
Parallelism draws from the same allowance
Anthropic introduced the public beta on September 17 for Pro and Max subscribers who joined the waitlist. Team and Enterprise plans remain unsupported. Eligible subscribers who lack access can still join the waitlist.
Projects carry no separate fee, but every worker consumes the subscriber’s existing Claude Code allowance. Anthropic limits accounts to 200 new threads per day across all projects. A thread that reaches a usage limit pauses and resumes automatically when capacity becomes available.
Project usage appears separately in the usage controls, and developers can choose the model and effort level for the coordinator and worker threads. New projects default to Opus for both roles, with low effort for the coordinator and high effort for workers. Several high-effort sessions running at once can exhaust plan limits faster than a single Claude Code session.
Where many threads pay off
Projects fit engineering work that can be divided into independent tasks and reconciled through branches and pull requests. Anthropic’s examples include:
- Performance work: Assign separate threads to profile endpoints, test optimizations, and open pull requests. A target such as p75 checkout latency refers to the response time at or below which 75% of requests finish.
- Cross-repository migrations: Connect API, web, and mobile repositories, then create one thread per codebase and report the required merge order.
- Batch changes: Distribute refactors, dependency upgrades, test repairs, or bug-triage items across parallel sessions.
Tasks with strict dependencies still require developers to sequence pull requests and resolve conflicts. Projects also remain cloud-only and limited to Claude Code, while parallel workers draw from the same plan limits. Small changes that fit one branch and one context window generally consume fewer resources in a regular Claude Code session.

Qwen3.8 - How to Run Locally
Guide to running Qwen3.8 quants including Qwen3.8-27B on your local setup.
Qwen3.8-27B is a 27B parameter dense model Qwen, featuring vision and reasoning capabilities, a 256K context window, and runs locally on 17GB RAM/VRAM setups. Qwen3.8 excels at agentic coding, vision and chat tasks, and can now run via Unsloth GGUFs, NVFP4 and Unsloth Desktop.
Nov 11 Update: Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs now use Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 which improves average accuracy by 5-10% accuracy at comparable sizes including Terminal Bench, DeepSWE and more benchmarks. We're working on an even better version of Dynamic quants which will be applied to Qwen4 and future models.
Thank you Qwen for day zero access. Unsloth quants also include:
- Developer Role Support for agentic tools like Codex
- MTP enabled for fast inference
- Tool calling: Improved parsing nested objects to make tools succeed more
Unsloth quants: Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF
Dynamic V3.1 Update (November 11th 2026)
We're excited to release new Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs using our updated Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 (preview) algorithm which improves Unsloth quants by 5-10% accuracy at the same size on most benchmarks and is the best in class for most tasks including coding, agentic workloads and general chat.
Most quants from 2bit until 6bit are updated. We found 3bit UD3 quants to do on par with UD3.1, so we do not update them. We are actively working on making all quants better!
We ran agentic benchmarks including Terminal Bench 2.1, DeepSWE v1.1, and general benchmarks like LiveCodeBench v6, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, AIME25 and many others. Run Qwen3.8
